They said they wouldn't do it. A touchscreen MacBook has been rumoured since the dawn of time (well, the noughties), but, in a quote that's been infinitely dredged up across the internet over the last couple of weeks, Steve Jobs himself decried the concept as "ergonomically terrible". But Jobs also famously asked, "Who wants a stylus?" And the answer among millions of Apple Pencil users seems to be a resounding, "Us!"

And after a few days with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, I'm happy to report that this is very much a device—perhaps even the ultimate device—for creatives. But rather than the ability to touch the screen, it's all about the quality of that 'PROLED' display itself. Turns out there's a reason Apple decided to lead with that, and not touch, in the name of the device.

Simply put, it's the best laptop screen I've ever seen. With up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, 10,000,000:1 contrast, and P3 + Adobe RGB colour, this is a best-in-class display that puts every other OLED laptop screen I've used to shame. It gives creatives a portable reference-quality display, which means it recreates video, colour and contrast as faithfully as possible. Once you've used the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, everything else looks washed-out in comparison, and for that reason alone it's impossible not to recommend for creatives – so long as the small matter of the $2,899 starting price isn't a barrier.

When it comes to touch, as I've written before, in my testing I've found it to be a nice-to-have rather than a need-to-have. Now that we're all touchscreen natives (which wasn't so much the case when Jobs made those comments in 2010), certain navigational actions just feel right, even on a laptop. Scrolling through windows, pinching to zoom in on a photo or map, scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro; there are plenty of times when touching the screen feels more intuitive than reaching for the trackpad. And Apple's subtle UI tweaks, such as having navigational icons expand when touched, make the whole thing feel more natural.

But equally, there were plenty of times when I preferred to use the trackpad – particularly when a certain level of accuracy was required. And despite Apple claiming to have produced a newly designed hinge with greater stability, it still wobbles. There's just no getting around the fact that a touchscreen on a vertical display is less ergonomic than it is on a flat one.

From a design perspective, the new MacBook Pro isn't a game-changer – unless you really missed the illuminating Apple logo (another noughties mainstay). There are improvements here and there; the Dynamic Island takes up less space than the notch, and slightly smaller bezels result in slightly larger viewing areas. But perhaps the most meaningful design change is the reduction in weight. That OLED panel has allowed for a 14% weight loss – making the 14-inch model, somewhat ironically, lighter than the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air.

But everything pales next to the screen. The PROLED XDR looks incredible. If you're looking for the most impressive visual fidelity available on a laptop, here it is. You can touch it if you like.

#9221. The Most AI-Paranoid States in the US Revealed

The Most AI-Paranoid States in the US Revealed

Wyoming is the most AI-paranoid state in the U.S., recording 4,700 annual searches per 100,000 residents. Vermont ranks second with 4,300, followed by Alaska with 3,600.

Wyoming tops the ranking with 4,681 annual AI-related searches per 100,000 residents, narrowly ahead of Vermont’s 4,292. Despite their relatively small populations, the two states generate 27,000 and 27,600 searches a year, respectively.

Alaska ranks third with 3,599.7 annual searches per 100,000 residents, followed by North Dakota (3,466) and South Dakota (3,113). Delaware (2,727) takes sixth place, while Rhode Island, Montana, Maine, and New Hampshire complete the top 10.

Population has a significant impact on the rankings. California generates the most AI-related searches overall, with 464,400 annually, but ranks 25th when adjusted for population, at 1,175 searches per 100,000 residents. New York and Texas each record 308,400 annual searches, but rank 13th and 28th, respectively, with rates of 1,527 and 1,058 per 100,000 residents.

Healthcare is the biggest source of AI-related concern, with the term “AI in healthcare” generating 21,400 searches a month, or more than 250,000 annually. Fears about an AI takeover of the world rank second, attracting nearly three times less search interest.

Concerns about AI taking over the world also appear to outweigh questions about its impact on employment. The phrase “will AI take my job” receives nearly five times fewer searches than “will AI take over the world” annually. Employment remains a recurring concern, however, with questions about AI replacing doctors and programmers generating a combined 21,600 searches a year.

The term “superintelligence,” which has recently entered wider public discussion, also features in the data, attracting 45,600 searches annually. However, it remains a relatively niche topic, with twice as many searches for “will AI take over the world.”

#9219. Weather Camera Captures 20-Year Timelapse of Skies Above New Zealand

Weather Camera Captures 20-Year Timelapse of Skies Above New Zealand

A New Zealand weather camera has captured a remarkable 20-year time-lapse showing two decades of changing skies over Lower Hutt — a city close to the capital of Wellington.

Trevor McGavin’s south-facing Lower Hutt weather camera has been recording 640 x 480 pixel images since June 24, 2000.

The timelapse, published by Peter McGavin, is made up of one low-resolution photograph taken at noon every day, played back at 25 frames per second; each second represents 25 days.

The camera was originally installed in the late 1990s to display local weather conditions on McGavin’s website. However, he explains on YouTube that he has been unable to recover any saved images from before 2006, meaning the timelapse covers approximately 20 years rather than the camera’s entire lifespan.

The footage was captured using a 1990s-era StarDot Technologies WinCam Live camera, which records images at 640 x 480 pixels through a serial RS232 interface. Despite being exposed to the elements for decades, the camera is still operating in 2026.

McGavin says the footage has been processed to reduce flicker and restore more natural colors. However, the processing has also contributed to an apparent lack of sunshine in the video, with some viewers questioning why the skies appear persistently cloudy.

He explains that several factors create this impression. The deflickering process blends cloudy frames with sunny ones, while the extremely fast playback makes individual weather changes difficult to distinguish. The camera’s aging CCD sensor has also gradually lost its sensitivity to blue light, making clear skies appear gray. Dirt accumulating inside the lens has further contributed to the hazy appearance.

These effects become more pronounced toward the end of the video. McGavin points out that Lower Hutt actually averages more than 2,000 hours of bright sunshine annually, adding that sharp shadows visible throughout the footage are evidence of sunny conditions.

The timelapse also offers a glimpse of seasonal changes in the Southern Hemisphere, where seasons occur at opposite times of the year compared with the Northern Hemisphere.

Other details are less immediately obvious. The black cylinders visible on the roof are rain gauges, while the trees in the background include native New Zealand species such as totara and pohutukawa, which retain their leaves throughout the year.

Snow is particularly rare in Lower Hutt. McGavin says the only snow to settle on the ground during the 20-year period fell on the afternoon of August 15, 2011, and had disappeared by the following morning.

The MovinkPad 11 comes with the Pro Pen 3, a paper-like screen, and a protective case, and the bundle now costs less than the tablet alone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve tested a fair few drawing tablets over the years, and while the iPad is still the default for many digital artists, Wacom is clearly keen to lure creatives away. The MovinkPad 11 is one of its more interesting attempts, and this deal is a good excuse to take a look.

Wacom is selling the MovinkPad 11 with a case for £402.70 with the code CASE20 at checkout. That’s down from £469.96, a saving of £67.26 (around 14%). The tablet alone is listed at a discounted £429.98, so you’re paying less for the tablet and case together than for the tablet by itself. It’s a handy extra, too, on a tablet that’s made to be tossed in a bag and used anywhere.

The MovinkPad 11 is built around the Pro Pen 3, not a generic Android slate with stylus support bolted on. The 11.45-inch display has a 2200 x 1440 resolution and a 90Hz refresh rate, and the screen is etched glass. If you’ve ever drawn on the slick glass of a regular tablet, you’ll know it can feel like sketching on a bathroom mirror. The textured surface adds a little grip and feels much closer to paper.

The Pro Pen 3 offers 8,192 levels of pressure sensitivity and 60-degree tilt recognition, and it needs no battery or charging. Those numbers look good on a spec sheet, but what I notice more is how naturally it responds to light pressure and follows your strokes.

It runs Android 14 with 8GB RAM and 128GB storage, so you don’t need a computer. You can download drawing apps such as Clip Studio Paint, and Wacom includes a two-year Clip Studio Paint DEBUT licence.

It isn’t the most powerful Android tablet around, and the screen suits sketching and illustration better than big professional workflows, but for that exact art need, it's a better choice than an iPad Air. It’s a portable digital sketchbook, and at £402.70 with the case, it’s easy to recommend.

Wacom’s premium MovinkPad Pro 14 is now 14% off too, and with its protective cover, it's a similar deal, saving £140.05. As my MovinkPad Pro 14 review found, its gorgeous OLED screen and Pro Pen 3 make it a serious iPad alternative.

#9216. New iPhone and iPad App Lets Filmmakers Control Up to Four Canon and Sony Cameras At Once

New iPhone and iPad App Lets Filmmakers Control Up to Four Canon and Sony Cameras At Once

Italian filmmaker Claudio Ripalti released Director Mode, a new iPhone and iPad app that lets videographers monitor and control up to four wirelessly connected cameras. As of now, the app works with a wide range of Canon and Sony bodies.

As of writing, Director Mode works with many Canon cameras, including the C50, C70, C80, C300 II, C400, and C500 II EOS Cinema cameras. The app is also compatible with the Canon EOS R1, R5 II, R6 II, R6 III, R6V, R8 II, R8, R50V, and PowerShot V1.

On the Sony side, compatibility is similarly wide. The app works with the FX2, FX3 (FX3A), FX30, and new FX5. It also works with Alpha-series bodies like the a1, a1 II, a9 III, a7S III, a7R VI, a7 V, and a7C II.

Once a camera is connected to Director Mode, the app can do all sorts of things. It includes live monitoring with camera telemetry, recording controls, and settings controls. It also includes “pro” monitoring tools like waveform, focus peaking, frame guides, anamorphic desqueeze, LUT monitoring, custom LUT import, touch focus and control, and more. Users can monitor and change ISO, shutter speed (angle), aperture, exposure compensation, and white balance, as NewsShooter explained in its coverage of the beta version last month.

Speaking of “pro,” while Director Mode is free to download and use with a basic membership, the full suite of features requires a paid upgrade. Director Mode Pro is $29.99 for lifetime access to all features.

While it’s compelling enough for people to use their iPhone or iPad as a real-time remote and monitor, Director Mode can do a lot more than control one camera. In fact, the app can show live feeds from up to four cameras side by side, each with monitoring and controls. This also works with a mixed-camera or mixed-brand workflow, meaning users can monitor and control a Canon EOS R6 III and R6 V alongside a Sony a7 V and FX5.

“On a small set, the person watching the image is often the one adjusting a camera and calling the take,” says the app’s developer, Claudio Ripalti. “Director Mode lets a solo operator run a multicamera setup from an iPhone with great ease.”

Director Mode is available now on the Apple App Store.

#9215. Sirui’s Affordable Aurora Series Goes Wider With 15mm f/1.6 and 24mm f/1.4 Primes

Sirui’s Affordable Aurora Series Goes Wider With 15mm f/1.6 and 24mm f/1.4 Primes

Sirui has announced the Aurora 15mm f/1.6 and 24mm f/1.4 wide-angle lenses for full-frame mirrorless cameras.

These fast, autofocus-equipped wide-angle lenses are designed for both photographers and videographers, promising reliable autofocus and high-end image quality across a wide range of scenarios.

Despite its ultra-wide field of view, the 15 mm f/1.6 lens promises very low distortion. Sirui says it is well-suited to architectural photography, travel, vlogging, and night shooting. The fast f/1.6 aperture should also enable more creative options for shutter speed and ISO.

The company says that distortion control has been a key focus for the lens’s design. Ultra-wide lenses can often make straight lines appear curved, especially near the edges of the frame. Sirui promises it has minimized these issues with its new lens, making it “particularly valuable for architecture and interior photography, as well as video production, where reducing distortion can also mean less correction and cropping in post-production.”

Inside, the 15mm f/1.6 lens features 17 elements arranged in a dozen groups. It includes three aspherical elements, three ED elements, and four HRI elements. The lens includes an 11-bladed aperture diaphragm, and its dedicated aperture control ring can be de-clicked for smoother operation during video recording.

Further, unlike some ultra-wide lenses, the Sirui Aurora 15mm f/1.6 accepts standard front 77mm filters. The lens is 106.4 millimeters (just under 4.2 inches) long and weighs 540 grams (19 ounces). It can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet), for a max magnification ratio of 1:12.5.

For those needing a bit more reach, the Aurora 24mm f/1.4 lens should work well for many of the same applications as the 15mm f/1.6, plus environmental portraits and scenes with more natural perspective. It offers a similar experience to the existing Aurora 35mm f/1.4, albeit with a wider field of view.

“Its 24mm focal length provides a wider view than a traditional 35mm lens without the exaggerated perspective often associated with ultra-wide lenses,” Sirui says of its new lens.

The 24mm f/1.4 includes some features tailor-made for video applications, including a de-clickable aperture ring, stepless aperture control, and minimized focus breathing. Like the 15mm f/1.6 lens, the 24mm f/1.4 prime has an STM autofocus system that promises quick, quiet focusing, plus support for eye-tracking and subject-detection AF modes.

The Aurora 24mm f/1.4 lens is 106.6 millimeters (4.2 inches) long and weighs 550 grams (19.4 ounces). It accepts 62mm front filters.

The 24mm f/1.4 includes 14 elements in 11 groups. There are three aspherical elements, four ED elements, and three HRI elements. Like the ultra-wide prime, the 24mm f/1.4 also sports an 11-bladed aperture.

Both new Sirui Aurora lenses feature a weather-resistant design and are available for Sony E, Nikon Z, Leica L, and Fujifilm X. However, only the E- and L-Mount versions are available now, with the Z- and X-mount lenses slated to arrive in Q1 2027.

Many 24mm f/1.4 lenses are on the market, including premium options from Sony (FE 24mm f/1.4 GM, $1,498) and Sigma (24mm f/1.4 DG DN Art, $879). Another Chinese-made competitor is the $589 Meike AF 24mm f/1.4. Sirui is the cheapest of the bunch, priced at just $499.

As for the new Sirui Aurora 15mm f/1.6, it is the only lens with that exact focal length and aperture combination on the market, but there are 14mm lenses like the Sony FE 14mm f/1.8 GM ($1,598) and Sigma 14mm f/1.4 DG Art ($1,839) to consider. There’s also the Sony FE 16mm f/1.8 G ($898) and Viltrox AF 16mm f/1.8 ($580), which are much closer in price to Sirui’s new option. The Sirui Aurora 15mm f/1.6 is $599.

Sony has revived a cult classic of 80s tech design, and retro fans are foaming at the mouth. Wired EarPods have been having quite the style resurgence, spotted on celebrities like Bella Hadid, Harry Styles and Zendaya (check out @wireditgirls on Instagram for more). #9213. The Go Front Pack From Moment Always Keeps Your Gear Within Reach

The Go Front Pack From Moment Always Keeps Your Gear Within Reach

Moment has announced the Go Front Pack, a small sling bag that the company says was inspired by hydration and running vests. It mounts on the user’s chest, giving them immediate access to a phone, lenses, filters, and cables without bouncing when the wearer moves.

The bag continues the trend of wearing front-facing small bags. Moment included a quick-access front phone pocket with a bungee hook to secure a phone while leaving the camera lens unobstructed, allowing creators to film while wearing the Go Front Pack. The phone can also easily be removed when needed.

“Shoot with your phone out front: a magnetic pocket with a bungee hook holds your phone, lens and all, on the outside of the bag, so you can film on the move. Travel with it: it’s light and weatherproof, with a hidden AirTag pocket inside the main compartment,” Moment says. “Carry it every day: stretch mesh pockets keep your cables, filters and lenses organized, and stashable wings let you wear it over your left or right shoulder.”

Moment employed what it calls a “no bounce” interior organization system that uses stretch mesh pockets for gear so items don’t jostle or bounce around while the bag is being worn, even during bouts of strenuous activity. A dual-wing design at the bottom of the pouch promises to give wearers a comfortable, body-wrapping fit when worn over either the left or right shoulder. The three-point strap, which keeps the bag snugly against the wearer’s body, can be removed easily.

The main compartment opens wide, though not so far that gear easily falls out, while on the larger Go Big size, a back compartment can hold a Moment SuperCage or iPad mini.

The exterior of the bag is made from Moment’s LightWeave Ripstop fabric, which features a dual-layer PFAS-free DWR coating to protect against water without feeling bulky. Moment says that a magnetic flap deflects water from the front-access zip, which the company notes reduces water ingress even in heavy rain.

The Go Front Pack comes in two sizes: a one-liter Go Small and a two-liter Go Big, the latter of which (as mentioned) can fit up to an iPad mini. Both are available starting today in either black or desert colors for $70 and $90, respectively.

#9212. Swedish museums restitute objects to Nigeria and Bolivia

Signing at the handover ceremony. From left: Nkechi Adedeji, managing curator of the National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM), Olugbile Holloway, director general of NCMM, Britta Söderqvist, superintendent of SMVK and Anna Westerholm, Swedish ambassador to Nigeria

Swedish museums last week began returning dozens of statues stolen by British troops from the Kingdom of Benin as well as sacred objects looted by grave robbers in the 1970s in Bolivia.

Three years after the Swedish government—at the time backed by the far-right Sweden Democrats—agreed to two restitution requests, the National Museums of World Culture (SMVK) began the final phases of enacting them.

At a ceremony in Lagos, 39 Benin objects were formally restituted to Nigeria, while according to Swedish media, 77 objects from the Niño Korin village—including the skull of a Kallawaya healer— were taken from storage in Gothenburg to be transported to the National Museum of Archaeology in La Paz.

The Bolivian objects, dating to around 600 to 1000 AD, the Tiwanaku period, were looted by locals in grave robberies in the 1970s and were later sold to the museum, according to the SMVK website.

A wiphala, or multi-coloured flag, from Niño Korin, is one of the objects in the process of being restituted to Bolivia

The African objects are some of thousands that were violently looted by British troops in 1897 from the Edo people in the old Kingdom of Benin, located in what is now Nigeria. They were later acquired by the former Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm. Six will remain in Sweden as part of a ten-year loan.

The restitution process began, according to the SMVK, after “clear signals from the Nigerian authority, the National Commission for Museums and Monuments, that they would welcome the return of all objects.”

Michael Barrett, the curator for Africa at SMVK, was in Lagos for the ceremonial signing-over of the 39 cultural objects, known as Emwin Arre. “I hope [this] is part of a broader shift in how our museums relate to the world around us,” he tells The Art Newspaper on his return.

“For too long colonial legacies of violence, theft, and exploitation have stood in the way of museum practices that are more responsive to a wider set of stakeholders, not least communities who have cultural and historical ties to our collections. Returning violently looted belongings to their communities of origin is a necessary first step.”

The process, he adds, is also part of earning the trust of modern audiences. “A focus on these relationships must be a central part of our practice going forward,” he adds. “At least if museums with ‘world collections’ are ever to live up to their potential [as] places where visitors may learn about humanity’s cultural achievements and many ways of being- in-the-world, in an environment defined by respect, empathy and curiosity.”

The Swedish restitutions follow a trend among European countries to return art and objects looted or obtained unethically from around the world. In 2022, Germany handed over a substantial collection of Benin bronzes to Nigeria. The Netherlands returned 119 similar objects in 2025 and the Dutch Museum de Fundatie returned an additional Benin bronze plaque last month.

While Cambridge University returned legal ownership of its collection of 116 objects to Nigeria in February, the British Museum last year ruled out the imminent restitution of stolen treasures, suggesting “collaboration” instead.

Staffan Lundén, researcher at the University of Gothenburg’s School of Global Studies, has studied the topic of “dealing with difficult pasts” and the British Museum’s collection of objects looted in Benin City. He says, by contrast, these restitutions were largely depoliticised in Sweden. “The decision was taken by the right-wing government,” he points out. “It is seen as common sense, moral justice and in line with the Swedish self-perception of being a progressive country which takes international responsibility.”

Around 160 institutions hold looted Benin artefacts, but how many are prepared to give them back? We asked museums in five countries for their position on restitution

As restitution momentum builds, director of Smithsonian’s National Museum of African Art says it could lead discussions for the return of looted Benin objects in US museum collections

#9211. Short Film Looks at the Photographers Shooting Gnarly Mountain Bike Photos

Short Film Looks at the Photographers Shooting Gnarly Mountain Bike Photos

Red Bull Rampage is one of the most demanding events in mountain biking, but the challenge isn’t limited to the riders. Photographers covering the competition must navigate steep, unforgiving terrain while carrying heavy equipment, often with only one opportunity to capture a defining moment.

A new documentary short from Pelican, Images That Last Forever: Photographing The Red Bull Rampage, turns its attention to the photographers documenting the event, including Christian Pondella, Paris Gore, and Bartek Wolinski.

Released to mark Pelican’s 50th anniversary, the film explores the physical and technical demands of photographing Rampage, drawing on the combined experience of three photographers who have covered the competition for decades.

Pondella, who is based in Mammoth Lakes, California, has photographed every edition of Red Bull Rampage since its inaugural event in 2001. This year’s competition was particularly significant, as it marked the event’s 25th anniversary and returned to its original site.

“They ride so much differently than they did back then. The sport has evolved, our photography has evolved in that time, the bikes have evolved, the riders have evolved, so over the 25 years, it’s drastic to change from where it started to where it is now,” says Pondella in the short film.

Having covered the event for so long, Pondella is now photographing riders who weren’t even born when he first started shooting Rampage.

“Hopefully in 25 years this will still be going on, and if it happens I’m going to be here,” he adds.

Paris Gore, a Red Bull photographer from Bellingham, Washington who PetaPixel has previously interviewed, has covered Rampage 13 times.

“Photographing Rampage is a pretty hardcore, physically demanding job,” says Gore. “You really have to run around, especially during finals. You could be on one side of the ridge and need to traverse the entire mountain. If you lose [your footing] you could fall off a huge cliff. But I love it.”

Bartek Wolinski, a photographer from Poland, is attending his 12th Rampage. He says he “always tries to follow the light before the action.”

“In general, Rampage is pretty difficult to photograph,” says Wolinski. “There is a lot of planning involved, but you have to be loose with your plan and adjust when it’s needed.”

#9210. Nuart Aberdeen 2026: Poetry In The Streets

Welcome to the latest edition of Nuart Aberdeen. As far as we can ascertain, this will be the first street art festival in the world with a focus primarily on poetry and text-based works. Over the years, for better or worse, the large scale colourful figurative mural has come to dominate the culture we work with, and although it’s an aspect of the culture we support, due to the resources required to produce murals, they’re perhaps also the least democratic form of art on the streets. As curators, researchers and producers working in “festival” culture, we have a responsibility to not only showcase and celebrate the most interesting and technically competent works of our time, but to also ensure the culture’s development and survival. The only way to do this, is to inspire and encourage those without the privilege of a fine art degree or access to the arts, to have a go themselves. This has always been Nuart’s primary goal, not just to produce art, but to also inspire and produce the next generation of artists. A lofty goal, particularly as it’s often in conflict with the stated needs of sponsors and partners, on paper at least, and no one stands in front of a Tower block mural and thinks, I’ll pop home and have a go myself on the gable end of Gran’s house.

What we do have evidence for, is that the smaller, more human scale works – the stencils and paste ups and interventions – do have this effect. You could say that the ease of copying a Banksy stencil, which requires no more than a craft knife, a piece of cardboard and an idea, is the very foundation of this culture. We’ve seen this happen time and time again. Indeed, several of the producers and artists joining us this year, started their artistic journey as assistants and volunteers at Nuart.

At Nuart, we’ve always prided ourselves on not only showcasing the BIG names in muralism, but on also using the festival as a place to explore and experiment with new forms and ideas that engage with the idea of the whole city as a canvas, and not just the wall. In this respect, Nuart Aberdeen have been fortunate enough to have the support of some of the most thoughtful and progressive partners that an event such as Nuart could possibly have, and this year is no different.

Whilst pondering this issue, how to balance the needs of partners, tourist boards, with the need to impress the public, and create works of curiosity and interest for scholars which inspire the next generation, I imagined a city without art on the streets, with no forms of public expression, where all art is concealed behind the walls of city institutions and under guard 24/7. And then I recalled a piece of graffiti sprayed on the walls of Paris during the 1968 student uprising, an event which saw waves of creative energy explode onto the streets. It read, “La poésie est dans la rue”, or “Poetry is in the Streets” – could we harness some of this energy at Nuart to revitalise and energise the culture?

A short while later, I remembered a quote from pioneering UK graffiti writer Mode2. He was discussing how graffiti culture had taken hold and blossomed in the UK in the 1980s, and in a throwaway quip had said, the reason it took hold was because regardless of how interested you were in making art at school, if you couldn’t draw or paint realistically, you were bottom of the class. Then graffiti came along, and it struck everyone that all you had to know to create and engage with it, was your ABC’s.

And that was it. It was these two quite innocuous events that formed the genesis of this year’s poetry and text based Nuart. These are forms of creative expression that we all have access to and I hope the festival sparks the public’s imagination in the same way that those early bubble letters and Banksy stencils did.

Thank you as ever to all of our sponsors, partners and to the city council, for allowing us once again to make a contribution to what we believe is a magical and inspiring city.

— Martyn Reed, Nuart Founder and CuratorArtists include: Alisa Oleva (UK) Ciarán Glöbel (SCT) dr.d AKA Subvertiser (UK) HICKS (UK) James Klinge (SCT) KMG (SCT) Molly Hankinson (UK) Remi Rough (UK) Robert Montgomery (SCT) The Rebel Bear (SCT) The Writing Is On The Wall (UK) Trackie McLeod (SCT)  V2k | (LT - SCT)

#9208. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

#9207. Over 50 Award-Winning Wildlife and Nature Photos From the 2027 NANPA Showcase

Over 50 Award-Winning Wildlife and Nature Photos From the 2027 NANPA Showcase

The North American Nature Photography Association (NANPA) has unveiled the incredible winning photos from its annual 2027 Showcase. The award-winning images show wildlife doing amazing things, stunning landscapes, and the most beautiful nature from around the world.

This year’s Best In Show winner is Texas-based nature and wildlife photographer Cissy Beasley, who won the top honor for her incredible shot of a frog catching a dragonfly in mid-air. It’s an exceptionally well-timed shot, with water droplets suspended in the air and the frog in a great pose.

“As we sat by a country pond, we watched a springy and ambitious Leopard Frog try his luck and skill at leaping up to snatch dragonflies from a perch or mid-air…over and over,” Beasley says. “Finally, he scored, securing an Eastern Pondhawk with his long, sticky tongue.”

Beasley’s photo also won the Macro / Micro / All Other category.

Alongside Beasley’s Best In Show victory, the NANPA Showcase 2027 recognized 249 other great nature photos, including winners across eight categories. The winners, runners-up, and Judges’ Choice honorees across all eight categories are featured below.

Charles Janson won the Birds category for his action-packed photo of a male Pileated Woodpecker hammering away at a dead Ponderosa Pine tree.

Over in the Mammals category, this year’s winner is Kevin Lohman. Lohman’s award-winning photo shows a pair of polar bears in Churchill, Manitoba, Canada, clashing with beautiful backlight. It’s a stunning silhouette.

In the ‘Scapes category, which is just a shortened version of landscapes, John Benford’s nighttime photo of Castle Geyser in Yellowstone National Park earned top marks.

The Best-In-Show winner Beasley also won the Macro / Micro / All Other category. Her winning photo is shown again here, alongside the first runner-up and two judges’ choice photos.

The Conservation category is an emotional mixed bag this year. While some of the awarded photos offer reasons for hope, the winning photo by Graham Gerdeman shows a dead Great Horned Owl lying face down in a puddle at a city cemetery in Nashville, Tennessee. It was the second Great Horned Owl found dead like this. No necropsy was performed despite the cemetery’s proximity to industrial sites.

Creative approaches to photography are encouraged in the Altered Reality category. The winning image by Dave Hattori has been heavily edited in Photoshop to create artistic special effects, while the first runner-up is a composite of 139 photos showing the consistent flight patterns of Gannets in Norway.

While not strictly focused on comedic wildlife photos like the Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards, the NANPA Showcase still offers plenty of laughs. This year’s winning photo by Kevin Lohman shows a seven-week-old Great Horned Owl fledgling looking shocked as a gray squirrel jumped at it. Lohman adds that although the owl did fall off its perch, it was thankfully unharmed.

While all the other categories focus on single image entries, the Series category asks photographers to submit seven photos related to a specific topic. In this case, photographer Parham Pourahmad’s winning series tells the story of how coyotes have adapted to more urban lifestyles and habitats in the San Francisco Bay Area. Pourahmad’s seven photos plus the seven shots from the three other winners are featured below.

Alongside the winning photos featured above, the 2027 NANPA Showcase judges recognized 250 works, including in the Top 100 and Top 250 galleries. All of these recognized photos are available to view on NANPA’s website.

You won't believe the gears are moving at the same speed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We've seen some impressive optical illusions here at Creative Bloq, from rotating horses to Mario on the moon and the existence or not of the colour purple. Yet still new ones come along that reveal new examples of how our eyes can deceive us.

In fact, there's a competition dedicated to the discovery of optical illusions, and it's recently revealed this year's winner. The Best Illusion of the Year Contest has bamboozled us before, and this year's choice is another mind bender, as you'll see in the video below.

Think the gear on the right is moving faster than the one on the left? Think again.

The winner of the Best Illusion of the Year Contest was submitted by Jacky Z. J. Yueh and Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco from the Perception and Cognition Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada.

Their video above shows two gears that are rotating at the same speed. But if you focus on the white dot on the left gear, you'll probably think that the other gear (the one on the right) is moving faster.

If you focus in the centre of the screen between the two gears, however, the effect disappears. You realise that they're moving at the same speed.

The explanation is that our peripheral vision is more sensitive to motion. This is due to specialised cellular structures and faster neural pathways in the retina and brain. This had a potential evolutionary advantage in that it helps us detect movement in the corner of our eye, which could alert us to a potential threat.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

But the winning experiment goes on to show that it's possible to confuse our minds even more. When the position of one gear is adjusted slightly to make it look like it is causally connected to the left one, and we again focus on the white dot, it now looks like the gear on the right is rotating even faster than before.

The conclusion is that perceived causal mechanics, even if they're not real, can altar our perception of dynamic properties, such as speed.

The Best Illusion of the Year Contest is a celebration of illusions and perception run by the Neural Correlate Society. It sees the study of illusions as critical to how we understand sensory perception, and many ophthalmic and neurological diseases too.

Previous winners of the contest have included a stunning Harry Potter Platform 9 3/4 optical illusion.

#9205. Artizlab Revives a Leica Classic for Just $400

Artizlab Revives a Leica Classic for Just $400

Artizlab has announced the Classic-M 1:1.4/50mm, a new 50mm prime lens that emulates the character and appearance of the classic Leica Summilux 50mm f/1.4 (E43) lens.

A vintage Leica Summilux-M 50mm f/1.4 E43 lens can fetch a pretty penny on the used market, easily costing thousands for ones in decent condition. Artizlab, like some competing companies on the market these days, hopes to capture the look and feel of a classic Leica lens in a package with a significantly more palatable price point. In this case, $399.

Like Leica’s classic lens, the Artizlab Classic-M 50mm f/1.4 is compact and lightweight. Although built from aluminum and brass, the lens weighs just 189 grams (6.67 ounces) and doesn’t obscure a rangefinder. It is 51.8 millimeters (just over two inches) long and accepts 43mm filters.

Speaking of rangefinders, the lens has standard rangefinder coupling and can focus down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet). However, with live view or when adapted to non-rangefinder cameras, the lens can focus as close as 0.45 meters (1.48 feet). This is a manual focus lens, as expected.

Artizlab notes that thanks to its closer minimum focusing distance, its new lens is “more than a faithful recreation” of a beloved vintage Leica.

“The classic is now closer than ever,” Artizlab says.

As for its optical performance, the lens includes seven elements in five groups and a 12-bladed aperture. The original Leica E43 has the same layout, but image quality and rendering are about more than just the number of elements and their placement inside a barrel.

“There’s a reason photographers have chased vintage Leica glass for decades — a certain warmth to the tones, a softness to the transitions, a way of rendering light that feels less clinical and more alive,” Artizlab explains. “We tuned the Artizlab Classic-M 50mm f/1.4 toward that same character: natural color rendition, gentle highlight roll-off, and smooth, creamy bokeh from the 12-blade diaphragm.”

Photographers shouldn’t expect extreme sharpness or resolution here, Artizlab warns. This lens is “not about being the sharpest” on a test chart. “It’s about the feeling in the photograph.”

For those who want that vintage-inspired look and Leica aesthetics without the Leica price tag, the Artizlab Classic-M 1:1.4/50mm is another option in an increasingly crowded market. At just $399, it’s a relatively affordable way for modern photographers to experiment with a different type of lens, one that certainly doesn’t conform to modern standards.

The Artizlab Classic-M 50mm f/1.4 lens comes in black and silver colorways and is currently sold out. It should be back in stock shortly.

#9203. New centre for contemporary Indigenous art launches in upstate New York

Branchline in Katonah, New York Photo: Denis Gutierrez-Ogrinc, courtesy Branchline

Branchline, a new 10,000-sq.-ft arts centre focused on championing contemporary Native American art, opened its main gallery to the public on Saturday (7 November). Located in the town of Katonah in New York’s Westchester County, Branchline is an initiative of the Gochman Family Collection (GFC), a private lending collection established in 2021 by the philanthropist Becky Gochman, who has a longstanding interest in Native art, and the former gallerist Zach Feuer.

Branchline is located steps from the Katonah station on the Metro-North Railroad, around 45 miles from Manhattan, and takes its name from a term for points where railroad tracks diverge and begin. When it is fully completed next year, the complex will span three adjoining buildings—including multiple galleries, a ceramics studio, two apartments, a deck filled with sculptures and a café.

Laura Phipps, a former associate curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, was appointed director of the GFC earlier this year. She is working alongside the creative director and curator Rachel Martin (Tlingít) and several other curatorial consultants at Branchline.

Installation view of Line Break at Branchline Photo: Denis Gutierrez-Ogrinc, courtesy Branchline

“Branchline builds on an extension of the ethos and the experience of the GFC, which is centring artists, supporting artists and sharing their work,” Phipps said at a preview of the centre on 5 November. “We were excited about all the ideas that Branchline conjures, both thinking about the metaphor of the train, the metaphor of trees, and what we can do to experiment and grow in this space.”

Organisers seek to explore innovative ways of activating the space in dialogue with the collection. The inaugural programme features a site-specific installation on the exterior of the main gallery building by the artist Matthew Kirk (Diné). The four-panel mixed-media work We Start To Think We’ve Got Someplace To Go (2026) features traditional Diné motifs made with construction materials.

The opening exhibition, Line Break, is curated by Branchline’s assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee/Diné) with the collection associate Nicole van Brugge. It explores the concept of lines and borders figuratively and metaphorically through nearly 30 works by 18 artists—including Sara Flores, Jeffrey Gibson, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, Kay WalkingStick, Marie Watt and Emmi Whitehorse.

A centrepiece of the opening show is the Diné artist Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021-24). It consists of abstracted musical scores that reference traditional Diné weavings while also evoking the sounds made by drones. The work is accompanied by isolated recordings Chacon captured of drones that hovered above the Standing Rock encampments during the Dakota Access Pipeline protests in 2016, with the lines in the work referencing the oscillating sonic waves of their erratic flight patterns.

Raven Chacon’s Storm Pattern (2021-24) Courtesy the artist and Sikkema Malloy Jenkins

Before establishing a dedicated exhibition space, some of the GFC’s holdings—totalling around 800 works—were displayed in private residences on Manhattan’s Upper East Side and in West Palm Beach, Florida. The GFC has loaned art to more than 100 exhibitions worldwide, with 260 works loaned to date.

Gochman and Feuer previously co-founded the Forge Project in 2021, an initiative similarly dedicated to the advancement of contemporary Native art and located around 70m north in Taghkanic, New York. That space also offers year-round exhibitions, artist residencies and workshops. It was converted from a private organisation into a Native-led nonprofit in 2024, when Gochman withdrew from the project. Candice Hopkins (Carcross/Tagish First Nation) is its current executive director and chief curator.

“We started Branchline and the Forge Project for social-justice reasons, and we are now separate from Forge, but we got the bug to collect Native art,” Gochman said at the preview. “The Branchline space functions as a free public space, which is a new concept for us. We are consistent, though, with the philosophy that artists and art come first, because we wouldn’t be here without them.”

“Interwoven Power” uses a fresh curatorial lens to change the way viewers engage with Indigenous art

The acquisition, from the collection of William P. Healey, will form the basis of an exhibition opening at the museum in August

The Gochman Family Collection has hired Laura Phipps as its director and will open a venue in Katonah, New York, this autumn

The gift from the John and Susan Horseman Collection will expand access to Native art across the US

From design work to watching movies, these are the best laptops for every kind of pasttime.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you need to buy a laptop for creative work, it's so important to get it right. Prices have climbed sharply this year, so you don't want to be saddled with the wrong thing..

Our top pick for graphic design is the MacBook Pro 14-inch (M6). It’s a brilliant all-rounder for almost any creative job. However, depending on what you need it for, other laptops are worth investigating too.

So in this article, I've highlighted the best laptops for a range of different tasks, based on hands-on testing by our reviewers using real design software. For further options, see our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best laptops for CAD.

The MacBook Pro has been the default laptop for designers for years, and nothing has yet changed that. The M5 model came first by a clear margin in our Photoshop benchmarks. Its screen is sharp and colour-accurate, and the battery comfortably lasts a working day. Now Apple has replaced it with the M6 version, which went on sale on 6 November.

We haven’t tested it yet, but it’s a spec bump rather than a redesign. Apple claims up to 30% faster graphics, and it adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Crucially, it costs the same as the M5 model, which rose to $1,999 / £1,999 in Apple’s June price rises.

So my advice is: either buy the M6 at full price, or pick up the M5 if you find it heavily discounted over Black Friday. Alternatively if money’s no object, Apple’s new MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display starts at $2,899 / £2,899 and adds a touchscreen. Our writer Daniel John called its OLED panel “the best laptop screen I’ve ever seen”.

The ProArt P16 is the best Windows laptop we’ve tested for creative work, and it's our top pick in both our laptop for CAD and laptop for animation guides.

If you're using CAD, the fact that this laptop runs Windows really matters. Revit and SolidWorks don’t run natively on macOS, while the P16’s Nvidia graphics and 64GB of memory give you plenty of headroom for large models. The built-in dial is handy for zooming and rotating, too.

If you're an animator, meanwhile, the star is the screen. It’s a colour-accurate OLED touchscreen, and as our reviewer Erlingur Einarsson says: “The 120Hz refresh rate is a welcome upgrade too, especially for animators and video editors.” The RTX 5070 also speeds up rendering in GPU-heavy tools.

The ASUS ProArt P16, in short, is pretty much everything a creative professional could hope for However, if you need even more power, ASUS also sells a version with an RTX 5090 and a 4K screen for $3,999.99.

The 16-inch MacBook Pro is the top pick in our 3D modelling laptop guide. You get a big, sharp screen, plenty of memory and the kind of battery life that 3D-capable Windows laptops can only dream of.

When our reviewer Rob Redman tested the previous M4 Pro model in Blender, Cinema 4D and Maya, he was impressed by its rendering speed and smooth viewport. “Simple things like dragging and dropping materials, which can be a little laggy on some systems, are perfectly smooth,” he says. The M5 Pro builds on that with a faster chip and Apple’s latest GPU cores.

Two things to bear in mind, though. First, if your pipeline relies on Nvidia’s CUDA or Windows-only plugins, you’re better off with a Windows machine. In which case, the Acer Nitro 16S AI is our best-value pick, while the RTX 5090 inside the Alienware 16 Area-51 is ideal if you need maximum rendering power.

Second, the MacBook Pro 16-inch (M5 Pro) is a lot of money, and the price climbs quickly once you add memory. If you have a lot of money, though, there's a very nice PROLED XDR version with a touchscreen costing $3,399.

Looking for the best laptop for Cricut? Then here's some good news. Cricut Design Space isn’t a demanding app, so you don’t need to spend a fortune on a laptop to use it.

Cricut recommends a minimum of an Intel Core i3 and 4GB of RAM, but 8GB is a more comfortable starting point, and 16GB will help with complex, multi-layer projects. The IdeaPad 5 2-in-1 gives you 16GB as standard, which is why it tops our Cricut laptop guide.

The 360-degree hinge is the clincher. You can fold the screen back into tablet mode and tap, drag and resize your designs directly on the screen. It also has a good range of ports, including USB-A, which is handy if you’re plugging in your cutting machine or a USB stick full of SVG files.

It’s a bit heavier than a regular laptop, and the screen isn’t the brightest or most colourful, but neither matters much for crafting.

The PZ13 is a Windows tablet with a detachable keyboard, and it’s the top pick in our drawing laptop guide. The big selling point is that ASUS includes the stylus, keyboard, stand and sleeve in the box, so the price you see is the price you pay.

The 13.3-inch OLED screen is bright, sharp and very colour-accurate, with a Delta-E of 0.3 in our testing. Battery life is excellent too, lasting over 20 hours in our video streaming test. “It’s unique and ideal for creatives,” says our reviewer.

It’s not built for processing power, though. Its Snapdragon chip is better suited to drawing and photo editing than 3D, and some Windows software, including InDesign, isn’t fully compatible with Snapdragon chips. So check your favourite apps run well on it before you buy. The glossy screen can also be reflective.

For most students, and certainly for creative ones, the MacBook Air is the laptop to get. It’s thin, light and silent, the battery easily lasts all day, and it has enough power for design, photo editing and light video work. “A thin and light laptop that performs as well as this will always be attractive to a creative audience,” says our reviewer Ian Evenden.

That power is the reason to choose it over the cheaper MacBook Neo. In our testing, the Air M5 was much closer to the MacBook Pro than the Neo: it scored 17,091 for multi-core performance in Geekbench 6, against 17,897 for the M5 MacBook Pro. In Photoshop, it more than doubled the Neo’s scores.

It’s not so cheap any more, though. Apple raised the price by $200 / £200 in June, although students can get quite a lot of money off through Apple’s education store. If you want to save cash and your course doesn’t involve creative software, the MacBook Neo at $699 / £699 is a great-value alternative, as long as you can live with 8GB of memory.

The MacBook Pro 14-inch (M6). It’s fast, has a superb screen, lasts all day on a charge, and it handles everything from design and illustration to photo and video editing. If you prefer Windows, the ASUS ProArt P16 is the best alternative.

It depends mainly on your software. Most design, photo and video apps run on both, and Macs win on battery life and build quality. But if you work in CAD, Windows is the safer bet, as Revit and SolidWorks don’t run natively on macOS. Windows laptops are also the only option for Nvidia graphics, which many 3D and rendering tools rely on.

For creative work, 16GB is the minimum we’d recommend, and 32GB is the sweet spot if you work with large files. You’ll only need 64GB or more for heavy 3D, video or AI work. Note that RAM on Macs and many thin Windows laptops can’t be upgraded later, so buy what you’ll need.

Not for graphic design, illustration or Cricut crafting, where integrated graphics are fine. For 3D, CAD, animation and video editing, a powerful GPU will save you lots of time, which means either an Nvidia RTX graphics card or a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or Max chip.

For drawing and Cricut work, yes. Being able to tap, drag and sketch directly on the screen makes both much more natural. For most other creative work, it’s a nice extra rather than an essential.

Cricut says that Design Space isn’t supported on Chromebooks, so we’d recommend a Windows laptop or a Mac. Some users run the Android version of the app on a Chromebook, but you may lose some features.

#9201. ‘The Odyssey’ Has Delivered Record Profits for IMAX

‘The Odyssey’ Has Delivered Record Profits for IMAX

IMAX reported its strongest quarterly financial performance in the company’s history last week, with record box office, revenue, and profits for the third quarter of 2026.

Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey drove the results, becoming the highest-grossing IMAX release of all time.

THR reports that the company generated $712 million in global box office during the quarter, a 90% increase year over year and a significant rise from the $372 million recorded during the same period last year.

The Odyssey accounted for more than $550 million of that total in worldwide IMAX box office, contributing more than 30% of the film’s overall theatrical earnings. Its success was supported by premium screenings, including 70mm presentations that attracted audiences to IMAX locations.

Revenue increased 64% to $175 million, compared with $106.7 million in the third quarter of 2025. Net income climbed to $117 million, up from $22.6 million a year earlier.

“These results demonstrate the significant operating leverage and opportunity as we further expand the network and grow Imax box office,” says IMAX CFO Natasha Fernandes.

Content solutions revenue increased 110% to $94 million, reflecting the rise in global box office, while technology products and services revenue grew 28% to $77 million.

IMAX CEO Rich Gelfond says the results represented a broader shift in audience demand for theatrical experiences.

“What IMAX achieved goes beyond simply a ‘great quarter’ and transcends the many records we shattered in the period. What we believe we are witnessing is an awakening to the power and potential of our platform to impact global culture, unlock new commercial opportunities, and inspire a new level of demand and awe in audiences around the world,” he says, per THR.

“Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey is a historic cinematic achievement crafted entirely with IMAX technology and its record-breaking success marks a new era of opportunity for our company. The record margins we generated in the quarter demonstrate the unique strength of our model, and the growing value of scarce events and experiences in an increasingly AI-driven world underscore a powerful opportunity for our business, as we look ahead to a remarkably strong slate over the next several years.”

The company expects to significantly exceed its previous full-year 2026 box office guidance of $1.4 billion, which would itself represent a record. Its expansion programme is also continuing, with more than 100 agreements for IMAX systems signed worldwide so far this year. Approximately 65% of those agreements involve new locations.

THR notes that IMAX is also exploring new auditorium formats, including smaller premium venues designed to offer audiences an immersive viewing experience through larger aspect ratios, greater depth of view and improved sound. Additionally, the company is considering adding between 10 and 15 new 70mm film locations in response to demand and the upcoming film slate.

#9200. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

I will finally have to make peace with Camera Control, and I’m not happy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whispers in the Appleverse suggest that the iPhone's Action Button could soon be a thing of the past, set to merge with Camera Control. As the tolerant yet unenthused owner of an iPhone 16 (the first line of models to include this feature), I must confess that the news has disturbed me. I can live without Cam Control, but the Action Button? She will be missed.

The iPhone 16 burst onto the scene with the promise that it was the latest and greatest iPhone for photography, and I lapped it right up. 2 years later, I have a confession. The Camera Control button and I rarely make contact, and when we do, we often fall out. My beloved Action Button could never.

I'll admit I was swept up in the initial glamour of the Camera Control button. Watching an Apple Genius effortlessly demo the tech had me fully indoctrinated. 'I will use that scroll feature every day', I naively thought. How efficient. How innovative.

Nowadays I tend to avoid the Camera Control button, having learned my lesson trying to use it at gigs. (Pro tip: balancing a drink under your chin while desperately trying to zoom using Cam Control can lead to major beer spillage if handled incorrectly). At times, I'll use it to make taking snaps a little easier, but on the whole, I scarcely employ the help of its various touch-sensitive capabilities.

But according to prolific leaker Instant Digital, I may have to get over my distaste for Cam Control, as future iPhone models will reportedly do away with the Action Button. Typically used to control the phone's silent mode, the Action Button can be set to an array of functions such as Focus, Voice Memo, Flashlight and more. Reports suggest this feature will soon be merged with Camera Control, supposedly streamlining these quick actions under one touch-sensitive roof.

Whether it's the simple functionality of the Action Button or the tactile haptic feedback of its gentle buzz, I find myself reaching for it far more than Cam Control. While I'll be sad to see it go, I'm intrigued to see how Apple will continue to evolve its iPhone models. It feels like the loss of the Home Button all over again, but I have mourned that and moved on. I'm sure I can do the same for the Action Button.

#9198. Photographer Killed While Capturing Vintage Airplane

Photographer Killed While Capturing Vintage Airplane

A photographer has died after she was struck by a vintage airplane that she was taking pictures of.

Pamela Haselton, 67, was attempting to move a tripod out of the plane’s path on Friday shortly after it had landed at a private airfield in Essex County, New York.

The 1942 Aeronca L-3 single-engine, two-seat aircraft had just landed and was taxiing toward its hangar. The aircraft was being flown by James Catalano, 77, who says he did not see the camera or Haselton before the accident.

Times Union reports that both Haselton and Catalano were from Wilmington, a small town located within Adirondack Park.

Police say that Haselton had been using the tripod to take photos of the Aeronca L-3, which she had positioned on the runway. When the plane touched down and approached, she tried to move the tripod.

An autopsy found that Haselton suffered massive injuries, and despite attempts to save her life at the scene, she was pronounced dead. Her death has been ruled an accident.

Tributes have been paid to Haselton, who, according to her friends, lived life to the full.

“Pam had a deep love for nature and the beautiful Adirondack region she called home. An avid hiker and passionate photographer, she was often out the door in pursuit of a beautiful sunrise, a breathtaking sunset, or another opportunity to capture the natural wonders around her,” the Town of Wilmington writes on Facebook.

“Whether exploring woodland trails, photographing mountain landscapes, or admiring the changing seasons, Pam found endless joy in the beauty of the world around her. Through her photography, she shared that beauty with countless others, inspiring an appreciation for the places she held so dear.”

According to Times Union, the Wilmington E. M. Cooper Memorial Public Library held an exhibition of her photos back in May. It also paid tribute to her.

“Pam was a treasured member of our Library Friends and a former board member. She was an absolute dynamo, with an infectious spirit and an energy that touched so many in our community.”

Hasleton’s friend Wendy Grossman tells Times Union that the photographer was the type to “climb a mountain at 3 AM to see the sunrise.”

“The whole community is kind of in mourning,” adds Grossman. “We’re grieving.”

#9197. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

Sign up at biltrewards.com. No annual fee, no hard pull for the initial application check. Once approved, download the Bilt app and register your rent payment address.

Add five small recurring charges to your Bilt card (streaming services, subscriptions, or small autopay bills). This ensures you hit the monthly minimum to earn points on rent without thinking about it.

Imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an important redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search shows availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:

Hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.
