Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. #9195. Leica Unveils Cine Play 1 Plus 4K Projector With 4,200 Lumens

Leica Unveils Cine Play 1 Plus 4K Projector With 4,200 Lumens

Leica has announced the Cine Play 1 Plus, an upgraded version of its compact 4K smart projector that increases brightness and contrast compared with its predecessor.

The Cine Play 1 Plus uses a Leica Summicron zoom lens alongside triple RGB laser technology and the company’s Leica Image Optimization (LIO) image processing system. It can project images measuring between 65 and 300 inches, with a maximum brightness of 4,200 ANSI lumens in Ultra mode.

Leica says the new model also offers an improved contrast ratio of 2,000:1, with the increased brightness designed to make projection more practical in rooms that aren’t completely dark.

The projector uses newly developed laser diodes and is designed for flexible use without permanent installation. Automatic image alignment and focus adjustment handle much of the setup process, allowing users to move the device between rooms or take it outside.

The Cine Play 1 Plus runs VIDAA 9.6, providing access to more than 400 pre-installed apps, including Netflix and Disney+, alongside free TV channels. It also supports voice control and features a dedicated Kids Zone.

Connectivity options include Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Apple AirPlay, HDMI, USB, and LAN. The projector is also compatible with smart home platforms including Apple Home and Control4.

An integrated sound system supports Dolby Digital and DTS Virtual:X for spatial audio. Leica says the system is designed to complement the projector’s large-format image without requiring a separate sound system.

The Cine Play 1 Plus features an aluminium housing with a glass front and aluminium rear panel. An optional Leica Floor Stand 1 is also available, allowing the projector to be positioned around a room. The stand uses an integrated pin-contact system to provide power without visible cables.

Leica says the projector is built using durable materials and energy-efficient technology. It also comes with a protective carrying case made from expanded polypropylene (EPP), which is fully recyclable.

The Leica Cine Play 1 Plus is available now in the UK, Europe, and selected Asia-Pacific markets, including Australia, through Leica Stores and authorized TV and home cinema retailers.

The recommended retail price is £2,550 in the UK, and €2,995 in Europe.

The game's parody brands have taken over Miami.

With under two weeks to go until the release of Grand Theft Auto VI for PS5 and Xbox, Rockstar Games has been cranking up the marketing for what's already the most-anticipated video game of all time. The publisher has been rolling out prominent billboards, bus wraps and digital placements globally (including a hand-painted GTA VI mural that was controversially "ruined" in Brooklyn).

Most of the advertising blitz uses familiar key art showing the game's two playable protagonists: Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval. But some of the best GTA VI ads don't show the game at all. in Vice City itself (that is, Miami, Florida), Rockstar continues to have fun with its many fictional parody brands, and the ads show just what a huge cultural event GTA has become.

“Rockstar is toning down their humor.” 💀 Meanwhile, GTA 6 ads on real-life public kiosks in Miami: 💀😭 From “Go Topless” to “Suddenly You Are Big Enough,” Rockstar is bringing Vice City’s unhinged humor straight into the real world. The double entendres, fake brands, and savage satire are STILL HERE. 💀🔥 GTA 6 isn’t toning down the humor. Rockstar is putting it on public display. 😂 Via: @GTAVI_Countdown #GTA6 #GTAVI #GrandTheftAutoVI #RockstarGames #ViceCityOctober 26, 2026

To the disappointment of all those real brands that are GTA VI trendjacking, Rockstar doesn't do product placement, and it's also quite selective when it comes to real-world collaborations. Instead, the game will feature hundreds of parody brands.

Some of these have crossed over into real world advertising, with billboards and digital displays cropping up in Miami for the likes of Crowex watches, Beige shapewear and Dix makeup. The game's takeover of the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center has even included outlets for the fictional fastfood chains Burger Shot and Cluckin' Bell.

Many of the ads continue Rockstar's penchant for using innuendo as a sharp social satire on real advertising, cutting through to real messages that brands are often communicating albeit in more euphemistic terms. "Always come early," the watch brand Kronos declares. "Suddenly You Are Big Enough," proclaims jewellery brand Kowalski on an ad showing a diamond-heavy engagement ring.

All the GTA 6 ads I saw on a kiosk in Wynwood (Miami). These shuffled between real ads 😂 https://t.co/l46q91OHRZOctober 19, 2026

It's been estimated that Rockstar's total global promotional costs could reach up to $200 million or even $300 million over the game's full launch cycle. I've seen some people wondering how much adverts for fictional brands like Dix and Juice Loose can contribute to the cause if it's not clear what they're promoting (there's a small logo and QR code in the bottom of some of them).

But this is what makes them so ingenious. They avoid traditional game marketing fatigue by showing the setting rather than the product. GTA is known for its satire of American consumer culture, and fictional companies, ridiculous slogans, and parody advertising are a core part of its identity. Putting these brands out there communicates the game's tone without showing a single mission or gameplay mechanic.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

By blurring the line between marketing and world-building, the ads also create intrigue among newcomers. When people see an advert for a bizarre fictional product with no obvious explanation, it generates curiosity and conversation, which becomes the marketing.

But, ultimately, they also reward existing fans who recognise names like Ammu-Nation, Sprunk, eCola, or other in-universe brands. For long-timer players, these are inside jokes that make them feel like they're being invited back into a world they love.

An advert for a kids' cartoon called Macca & Friends reads "Coming November 19 on Weazel”. The real message is clear to anyone who knows Weazel as the in-universe media company since GTA IV. This kind of advertising doesn't just promote a product; it makes people feel like they're part of the phenomenon. They deepen immersion, keep people talking and cement the game's status as not just the most-anticipated video game of all time but perhaps the most hyped entertainment product in any category.

#9193. Canada’s proposed federal budget includes tax breaks for artists and $554m funding boost for museums

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney Photo courtesy Prime Minister of Canada, via Wikimedia Commons

The proposed budget Canada’s Liberal government released on 5 November offers the country’s artists a lifeline, recommending new tax measures and funding channels. In a post on X, shortly after finance minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled the budget, the Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote that “if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to $45,000” ($31,800) of income from their creative work.

Much remains unknown about how this tax exemption and other measures would be implemented. The budget released last week only proposes a tax credit and the federal government has yet to set its cost, start date or eligibility rules. Ottawa says its planned consultations with Canadians and the cultural sector will be announced in the spring 2027 economic update.

The proposed budget also includes C$783.1m ($554m) over five years going toward the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada, the National Battlefields Commission and national museums, according to The Canadian Press. It also promises free entry to national museums for visitors under age 25, funded through a subsidy of C$46.3m ($32.8m) over five years, then C$11.5m ($8.1m) per year. The budget also calls for increasing funding to the Canada Council for the Arts with a new investment of C$20m ($14.1m) over three years.

“This funding falls far short of what is actually needed: permanent, stable funding at a scale that enables impactful support for Canadian artists and institutions,” Jenna Faye Powell, the interim national executive director of Carfac (Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des Artistes Canadiens), tells The Art Newspaper.

In addition to funding boosts and tax breaks for artists, the budget reiterates support for the long-promised adoption of artist’s resale rights in Canada, which would provide artists with royalties from secondary-market sales of their work. In the 2025 Budget, the government announced its intent to amend the Copyright Act to create an artist’s resale right in Canada, but the legislation never materialised.

Adopting an artist’s resale right “would provide creators of original visual artworks with a royalty each time their work is resold through an eligible sale, creating an additional source of income”, Carfac and the Regroupement des Artistes en Arts Visuels (RAAV) wrote in a joint statement. More than 100 countries around the world have artist’s resale right laws on the books, although neither Canada nor the United States has adopted such a policy despite multiple attempts.

“As a sector, we still have a lot of questions, while many artists need relief now,” Powell says. “Especially those still grappling with tariffs. Carfac will certainly push to be a part of that consultation process.”

For the Vancouver-based artist and pioneer of photo-conceptualism Ian Wallace, the proposed budget’s measures for supporting artists and the arts sector are welcome news. “Generous support of Canadian museums allowing them to build their collections by purchasing the work of emerging artists” is an important part of development of contemporary Canadian art history, he says, as is academic research and discourse around contemporary Canadian art.

Wallace adds that the tax credit is a “generous one”, although he says that “most Canadian artists are not selling more than C$45,000 a year in any case” and their yearly taxable income fluctuates wildly.

“When Canadian artists are doing their, work it’s not just to get by and pay the rent,” Wallace says. “It’s to contribute something to the overall culture. That’s the value of it: to show that there is a valuable cultural history in Canada that we are proud of and can articulate.” He adds: “I’m happy to see that artists and what they’re doing is respected and supported in the federal budget.”

As for the artist’s resale right legislation, Wallace has a more nuanced outlook. The law would apply to secondary-market sales that occur “outside of the normal sale structure that happens through a gallery that represents the artist”, he says. “In that sense, suddenly there’s another legal structure to deal with that might or might not be work well. I’m obviously for anything that supports the artist, but I can see some more bureaucratic and financial complications coming up with the artist’s resale right.” But, he adds, that is “more of a problem for collectors and institutions than artists”.

The recently passed federal budget includes a pledge to provide artists royalties when their work is resold on the secondary market

The move would be especially significant for First Nations artists, who make up an enormous share of Canada’s art market but rarely earn more than subsistence income from sales

#9192. Photoshop Now Relights and Restyles Your Photos Using AI

Photoshop Now Relights and Restyles Your Photos Using AI

Today at Adobe MAX 2026 in Miami Beach, Adobe announced a wide range of updates to its core applications and technologies, including Photoshop and Lightroom.

One of the key new features inside Adobe Photoshop is Relight. This is not necessarily a unique concept, as plenty of other apps and plugins have promised a similar concept: Fundamentally changing the “light source” in a photo with toggles and sliders.

Adobe says that Relight in Photoshop can dynamically add new light sources that naturally and non-destructively blend into the scene. Users can adjust the position, color, and brightness of their software-generated lights.

In a similar vein, the new Generative Restyle uses generative AI to turn text-based prompts into a new layer. Photographers can type how they want to style their image, and the AI does the rest. Well, mostly, as the intensity of the effect is still controlled manually via a slider.

Some familiar tools are getting major tweaks. For example, the Remove Tool is receiving a new “related elements” function. This automatically detects associated surrounding elements around an area the user paints over, including footprints, reflections, and shadows. It should be a time saver.

Likewise, a new Quick Compare makes it easier to see the before and after results for edits, rather than making users toggle between different states inside Photoshop.

AI Assisted Editor is not new, although it remains in beta inside Photoshop. The AI Assisted Editor is getting some big changes. There’s a new Camera Angles (beta) tool that lets users explore new viewpoints and perspectives inside an image. There’s also Generative Recompose that repositions and image into a new aspect ratio while promising to preserve the general composition. That could be useful for people trying to fit a landscape image to portrait orientation for social media. There’s also a tool to Convert to Text Layers, which extracts text from a flattened image and converts into an editable type layer.

Remove Ambient Effect Only sounds promising. It promises to remove distracting atmospheric effects, like lens flare, haze, or reflections, without removing any objects in a photo. If it works well, it could be a time saver.

Photoshop is also getting a new timelapse function that can turn the user’s entire creative editing process and workflow into a shareable timelapse video.

Over in Lightroom, there are many changes across the board.

Lightroom is getting in on the halation craze. A new Glow tool adds soft, cinematic light to photos. There’s a hazy Diffusion option or a “retro film-style” Halation tool. There are presets, although users can also fine-tune the effects to their preferences.

Blemish Removal, which was already in Lightroom on mobile, is now available in Lightroom on desktop. It includes new controls that Adobe says are suited to professional workflows and offers various fine-tuning options to ensure that only blemishes are removed, not natural elements like freckles.

Camera Tethering, a long-time area of dominance for Lightroom Classic compared to Lightroom, is getting a big update across Lightroom on Desktop and iPad. Adobe promises more ways to review, collaborate, and organize while shooting.

Finally, Open Eyes, arriving in public beta, can replace closed eyes with open ones. Adobe promises natural-looking results and the feature relies upon a reference image of the individual in the library, which Lightroom can find automatically. It’s not generating eyes from scratch.

While much of Adobe’s focus today is on Lightroom, rather than Lightroom Classic, Glow and Blemish removal are coming to Lightroom Classic as well, and the company promises some big news about other Lightroom Classic improvements and Adobe Camera Raw enhancements very soon, maybe even at MAX itself. There’s a lot going on in the Lightroom world right now.

#9191. Premiere Update Brings Color Mode Out of Beta, Plus Generative Video & AI Audio Tools

Premiere Update Brings Color Mode Out of Beta, Plus Generative Video & AI Audio Tools

Adobe is updating Premiere with a ton of AI-based tools and assistance as well as promising a new, wholly revamped approach to color grading.

The revamp to color grading has been in beta since last April but is now being rolled out to the production version of the software. Called Color Mode, it replaces the Lumetri Color Panel that has been Adobe’s approach to color grading for the last several years. This new color editor was touted as a “first-of-its-kind” color grading system and appears to be a direct response to the far more widely beloved system inside of DaVinci Resolve.

“Most Color Mode controls are bi-directional. Move your mouse up and down for one control, left and right for the other. Or press Shift for precise single-axis adjustments. Each control activates a unique heads-up display with scopes, numeric info, and real-time animated feedback that guides your creativity with confidence and clarity,” Adobe touts.

https://petapixel.com/assets/uploads/2026/11/Color-Mode.mp4

The company says that controlling this system is meant to be intuitive as “it works the way you think.” New bi-directional controls animate as they are used, and grading can be handled on single clips, groups, or entire sequences without layers.

“No more copying and pasting attributes. Actually understand how color is flowing through your timeline,” Adobe says.

Color Mode has been a point of discussion for months, but the other updates to Premiere are both newer and very much AI-based. Firstly, Adobe is deploying its Creative Agent, which is an AI assistant, into the video editor. The company says that this agent allows editors to direct and execute complex, multi-step workflows using natural language prompts. It can apply effects across every clip in a sequence, track masked subjects through a frame, and adjust color and exposure across an entire sequence simultaneously, for example.

Adobe is also adding a Generative Media Tool, which brings generative AI directly into a timeline to create missing video clips (like b-roll), sound effects, soundscapes, and background music. The AI behind it can be Adobe Firefly, but can also use the likes of Google, Kling, Runway, and Luma.

Adobe is also adding AI-powered audio tools that can clean up, separate, and refine audio. Premiere can now separate audio sources into stems that can be edited individually (a feature that was also recently added to Apple’s Logic Pro). Adobe says it is also capable of separating crosstalk, which means breaking overlapping speaking voices onto independent tracks.

Coming to the beta version, Premiere Pro is also getting a new Generative Remove tool that can remove objects from video (Adobe provides examples such as boom mics, logos, or background distractions). Editors can mask and track the object, and Premiere can fill the space with “realistic detail” while leaving the rest of the clip untouched.

Finally, as announced last week, Adobe is adding access to hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks for use in non-commercial videos.

“Music from UMG and WMG is available starting today in Premiere on iPhone for use in personal, non-commercial videos, with availability on Android coming soon. For projects that require commercially licensed music, you can continue to access Adobe Stock Audio,” Adobe says.

Adobe is also promising that the Agentic editing experience it is bringing to Premiere Pro will also be coming to Premiere Mobile “soon.”

Sci-fi and fantasy artist Calder Moore breaks down his process for creating a dark fantasy landscape into clear manageable tasks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In this tutorial, I’ll be doing an overview of the basic steps I take to create a compelling and highly detailed scene, from the basic sketch to rendering and adding post effects. I’ll also go over using basic geometry with displacement to really push the scene’s details and interest efficiently and quickly. I'll be using Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Octane Render and Photoshop (see our guide to the best 3D modelling software, and you might want one of the best laptops for 3D modelling).

Before diving into complex scenes like this, it’s a good idea to grab some inspirational images to build your visual palette; things like the architecture, environment, lighting, composition and mood. For these types of scenes, I like to pre-prep in 3D a bit, building up a library of foliage scatter systems and materials.

This allows me to create these complex scenes much faster and focus on the art, rather than get sidetracked with technical stuff. A fun fact for this scene: it wasn’t originally going to be greyscale. I turned down the saturation during the lighting phase to check values, and immediately got inspired to keep it that way, as it helped push that video was looking for!

Lastly, these scenes can seem extremely daunting to make. I find that the best approach is to write down all your tasks that you need to do to make it: make tower, break tower, make ground, detail ground, etc, so instead of seeing a big task, you see 20 very manageable tasks.

I’ll almost always start with a small sketch, as this allows me to quickly iterate on a few different compositions to see if any work for the kind of vibe I want to have, and also figure out the flow of the scene in general. In this case, I wanted to have an epic tower with that feeling of lonely, forgotten ancient power.

Once I have a sketch figured out for the direction, I go into Cinema 4D to establish the scene. Using basic geometry and sculpting tools, I build out the basic forms for the landscape and the silhouette for the tower.

During this process, I will also quickly establish the camera position. Locking it in early is key, and lets you refine the scene to that shot.

Now that the scene is blocked in, I can refine elements of it. For the tower, I’ll use displacement textures so I can stick to basic geometry. Using symmetry for archways and radial cloners for pillars, I build up the details for the tower elements, then use radial cloning to create the tower.

Now that we’ve built the tower, we can destroy it! Using various tools like the knife tool and voronoi fracture, I add cuts into the geometry. Loosely following the sketch, I then lasso-select portions of it and delete to remove the unwanted portions, making it look like it collapsed.

It’s good to spend a little bit of time on this step to make sure the damage feels natural.

Next, I’ll dive into the terrain element. Exporting that basic geo and bringing it into ZBrush, I’ll then sculpt more of the basic forms, refining the big shapes more. Using displacement texture on this terrain piece, I’ll keep the details light, as that will add a ton later.

I then create some quick UVs for it so the materials’ displacement doesn’t cause too much artifacting, then export back to C4D.

Now that we have our sculpt back in C4D, I’ll start building up the shader for it. Using a tileable photoscanned rock material, from RD Textures (now in Megascans), I build up a basic shader.

Cranking up the displacement scale for it, I’m able to add a ton of complexity and depth to that basic sculpt. Playing with the scale and UV offset settings, I can then find an interesting silhouette.

We have a basic terrain now, but the ground doesn’t quite feel natural, and this is where the power of displacement textures shine. I’ll duplicate the terrain geo and bring it up in Y a bit and sculpt some areas back down, then assign it more of a rocky ground/ photoscanned material instead of a cliff material.

In the render, you can see how we start to get a nice blend between the materials!

For the tower, I’ll start by creating a basic stone wall material – also with displacement – which helps a ton to add the details that the basic geometry lacked. To help break up that tiled stone material, I’ll then use a noise material that darkens areas to create some grime, and blend it into the material using the gradient marble texture so there’s more grime near the bottom of the tower.

This step is actually done in tandem with steps 7 and 8. For the lighting, I brought in a few HDRs to find a lighting scheme that I felt fit the vibe, and pushed the composition to be stronger, playing with light and shadow in the scene to create a stronger contrast, readability and visual interest.

Lastly, I added a cloud plane with intent to help the scene’s compositional flow.

Making many of these scenes I have a bunch of Octane Scatter systems set up with different trees, shrubs, grasses and plants. With these, I’ll take the terrain, and paint a vertex map to tell the scatter systems where to generate the foliage. In this case, I used my pine trees, shrubs and grass.

The last step in C4D is rendering out the final scene. With these heavy nature scenes, I usually work in portions so that I can see the results faster. During this step, I focus on adjusting the render settings and scene optimisation so I can get a big render fast.

Along with some last-minute scene tweaks, I’ll also render out some passes. These include a Z Depth pass, a Bloom pass and an object ID pass.

With everything rendered, I bring it all into Photoshop. First, I’ll go through the scene, and using basic brushes, paint over the artifacts from displacement and weird areas that don’t read nicely.

For this scene, I wanted to make that ‘old photo’ look, so I played with the levels and exposure to bring up the blacks, adjust the BG values and add that bloom pass.

Here’s a close-up of how I took the base rendered geometry and painted over it, removing those geometry artifacts, smoothing out some visual noise and adding brick details in the silhouette. You can also notice that I added a bit of blur to the BG parts of the tower. This helps the FG ones read a bit better and feel less flat.

Lastly, I added a couple old photo and paper textures on vivid light and multiply (though I played with the layer styles to find a good look), and on top of everything, did some last-minute levels adjustments to balance the scene with those textures layered on.

I also like to duplicate and merge everything down, then add a grain effect. This help get rid of that 3D look.

#9189. Adobe’s Creative Agent Wants To Do the Photo and Video Editing Tasks You Don’t Want To

Adobe’s Creative Agent Wants To Do the Photo and Video Editing Tasks You Don’t Want To

Adobe has been developing agentic AI for years, and at this year’s Adobe MAX in Miami, it looks like it has finally been fully unleashed. Adobe is ushering in significant expansions to the Adobe Creative Agent, which users can direct using text across not only Adobe’s Firefly AI platform but also Creative Cloud apps like Photoshop and Premiere.

The Adobe Creative Agent is designed to help users with complex, multi-step tasks across Adobe’s creative software. This agent works directly alongside Adobe’s expanded AI Assistants (beta) across its applications, including Photoshop and Premiere.

The overarching goal, as Adobe has discussed before, is to use AI for repetitive, tedious, or otherwise less creative tasks. For example, organizing files, generating masks, and replacing one color with another are all relatively uncreative tasks. The ideas behind these tasks, like why the user wants a specific object in their photo selected and what local edits to do it, are the artistic ones.

“Since its introduction earlier this year, creators have used it for everything from batch retouching portraits to converting product shots into short social videos. Creators remain in the director’s chair, guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve,” Adobe says.

Of course, Adobe has noted before and continues to say that it wants to create AI agent tools to empower its users, and then those users can decide how and when they want to deploy them.

“We’re powering a new era of creativity where creators and creative professionals at every experience level have the tools, models and agents they need to bring their biggest ideas to life and stand out with work that reflects their unique taste, style and vision, while staying in control of every outcome,” says Anil Chakravarthy, President and incoming Chief Executive Officer at Adobe.

“With demand for content growing across every format and channel, we’re delivering new innovations across our product portfolio that expand how creative work happens and put the power of Adobe’s tools within reach for even more creatives,” Chakravarthy continues.

Adobe’s new Firefly-powered agents can be always on, tasked with doing certain things as needed. For example, if someone needs to turn an image into a deliverable across different formats, the Adobe Creative Agent can do that thanks to new Photoshop tools like Generative Recompose.

The Adobe Creative Agent also works with other new AI-powered tools inside Photoshop and Premiere, like Relight and Generative Restyle in Photoshop and Generative Remove (beta) in Premiere.

Not every Adobe user necessarily wants to use Adobe’s own agent. They may already be using one in other applications. Today at Adobe MAX, Adobe also previewed local MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration, which will let creative pros direct their preferred third-party agent to make changes inside Photoshop, Premiere, and other Creative Cloud apps.

Adobe’s new AI Assistants, powered by the Adobe Creative Agent, are now available in beta in Adobe’s flagship desktop apps, except Photoshop, where the AI Assistant is available only in Photoshop (beta). Adobe’s local MCP integrations will be available in private beta early next year.

#9187. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9186. Hundreds protest US Senate bill that would gut key section of National Historic Preservation Act

Protesters, including members of tribal nations, at the US Capitol on 9 November to protest the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act Photo © Emma Cieslik

On Monday (9 November), hundreds of protesters gathered on the West Lawn of the US Capitol in Washington, DC, to protest the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA, or senate bill S.5653), which would gut a key section of the National Historic Preservation Act. Representatives from more than 100 tribal nations, members of congress, leaders from the Association of African American Museums, the DC Preservation League, the American Institute of Architects and the Archaeological Institute of America gathered to protest a bill that would remove the requirement for federal agencies to notify and consult with the public and tribal nations about potential harms to historic sites, as stipulated in Section 106, Title III of the National Historic Preservation Act.

The BAAJA, described by New Mexico congresswoman Melanie Stansbury at the protest as a “dirty deal”, was created without tribal consultation or public input. According to California representative Jared Huffman, the 500 new pages of legislative text, which he described as “the most sweeping legislation we’ve seen on energy and environmental policy in decades”, was released just 48 hours before the Senate was set to vote on it Monday evening.

“They scheduled this vote for tonight to try to prevent something like this,” Huffman told protesters gathered on the Capitol lawn; organisers estimated around 800 people attended. “To try to prevent the American people from having a say, from looking under the hood of this sweeping legislation and understanding what’s actually it, but you came anyway.” Holding signs with illustrations of President Donald Trump’s planned Triumphal Arch in flames and “Nix 106”, protesters gathered for over two hours to listen to more than 15 speakers who argued that BAAJA would seriously threaten US history.

The 9 November rally at the US Capitol against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act Photo © Emma Cieslik

Greg Werkheiser, a leader of the Section 106 Coalition and co-founder of Cultural Heritage Partners, kicked off the protest. “We gather at the seat of American democracy, where the laws of this nation are written, to affirm one simple principle: the people deserve a voice in decisions that affect the places that we love,” he said. “That is the promise we have come here today to defend.”

Along with removing the requirement for federal agencies to engage with the public, the BAAJA would also make consultation with tribal nations optional, narrow what types of activity trigger a federal historic preservation review, restrict the definition of what constitutes a historic site, and remove any consideration of sensory, indirect and cumulative effects of changes to historic and sacred sites, essentially allowing federal agencies to take over tribal and state historic preservation offices that do not abide by limits and deadlines that the new bill would set. The BAAJA would even restrict what legal action people and organisations can take against the destruction of historic and sacred sites.

“For tribal nations,” Arizona congresswoman Adelita Grijalva said, “the fight is more than historic preservation. It’s about sovereignty. It’s about self-determination. It’s about the fundamental right to protect our ancestral homelands, culturally significant sites, and traditions that have existed since time immemorial.”

Protesters at the 9 November rally at the US Capitol against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act Photo © Emma Cieslik

In its current form, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act requires federal agencies to consider the impact of federally funded building projects and requires that people receiving federal funds or permits consult with tribal nations. If passed, S. 5653 would make that consultation—the requirement that tribal nations participate in decision-making—optional.

“Our sacred places are living places of prayer, our responsibilities to them do not end at the reservation boundary,” Harry Antonio Jr, the governor of the Pueblo of Laguna in New Mexico, said at the rally. “You do not have to share our prayers to understand why those places deserve respect. Section 106 gives our governments a way to bring those concerns into federal decisions.”

Senators in favour of the bill have argued that its passage would lead to more economic opportunities. Articulating a position held by most rally attendees, Grijalva said: “Economic development does not require sacrificing our history, our culture or our sovereignty. We can create jobs without destroying sacred places. We can create jobs without sacrificing Mother Earth, our land, our water.”

Protesters at the 9 November rally at the US Capitol against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act Photo © Emma Cieslik

Rashida Tlaib, the congresswoman from Michigan, said the bill would be used to fast-track projects with severe environmental consequences, including data centres and gas pipelines. “This bill strips away what little tools we already have to defend ourselves from corporate polluters,” she said.

The senate’s vote on the BAAJA coincides with Trump’s push to build a 250ft-tall arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. On 5 November, protesters gathered at its proposed site and spoke against it during a National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) meeting. Although the NCPC voted to approve the arch, a Washington, DC judge then immediately blocked construction for 14 days.

“The court orders stopping construction of those projects would not be possible if this BAAJA legislation becomes law,” Huffman said. “If this becomes law, the administration will use that in those pending court cases to make it much, much harder to stop Trump from advancing those and other vanity projects.”

Speakers urged protesters to call their senators, and implored senators to vote down the bill or to table a vote until the newly elected members of congress are sworn in in January.

One group called the sudden demolition “a collective loss” while another expressed concern the $300m ballroom that will replace the East Wing “will overwhelm the White House itself”

#9185. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

It's becoming harder for indie developers to stand out on Steam amid all the AI slop out there, but one little gem has just shown that it's still possible to cut through the noise. Drawquarium is a game about drawing and looking after fish, and it's picked up thousands of wishlists in days – much to its developer's surprise.

Key to the viral success was a novel trailer that breaks a key rule but seems to have really captured people's imaginations in the current climate. It provides a sign of hope for other developers too, if only by showing that there's a still a big appetite for quirky games that display a clear human touch (if you're just starting your own developer journey, see our guides to the best game development software and the best laptops for game development).

Kaleb Lechowski's Drawquarium is an upcoming sandbox game that involves drawing your own fish and then feeding and raising it, and gradually building a cosy aquarium. You can then use your aquarium as an animated desktop wallpaper, if you want, and there are some built-in tools designed to help players focus or unwind.

Kaleb says he was inspired to develop the game because he wanted to bring his children’s drawings to life. That original impetus appears to also have inspired the fictional story of the trailer above.

A lot of people might say the trailer breaks a core rule by not showing any actual gameplay until past the halfway mark in what is a three-minute video. That might not normally be the most sensible way to promote a game, and it wouldn't work for everything. But in this case, the well-executed and emotive nostalgia marketing really paid off.

A post on Twitter has received over 128,000 likes, another over 100,000, and the game picked up 70,000 new wishlists in just a week. A lot of people are saying the trailer made them cry.

"Your trailer made me sob. It was way too relatable," one person writes on Reddit. "I can’t wait to play this little game. Thank you for putting your creativity into the world. We all need things like this that make us wonder in awe at the magic of nature, beauty, and art."

"Bro made a Cannes award winning short film to sell an indie game," someone writes on YouTube.

Kaleb has a background in 3D art for the film industry, and those storytelling skills clearly carry over to the trailer, which works as a self-contained story. But he was still surprised at how well it was received.

"What surprised me most was how strongly the message behind the trailer resonated with people," the developer comments on Reddit. "With AI becoming such a huge topic in gaming and art, it seems like people are really craving something made by humans, with genuine love and passion. I'm honestly overwhelmed and don't even know what to do with all these emotions."

You can download a Drawquarium demo on Steam. The full game is scheduled for release on 13 November.

Alas, the sudden attention has also brought with it the negative aspects of indie game success these days. Several unauthorised copies of the Drawquarium demo have been cropping up in the Google Play store, so make sure you check out the game via the official Steam page.

An effective environment is about much more than spectacular landscape.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve learned that an impactful environment is about more than just a beautiful image or a spectacular landscape: it acts as a character in its own right, capable of conveying emotion all on its own. Having started my career as a concept artist, I realised that environments don’t only serve as background for characters – they're a powerful narrative tool.

All visual elements I design must serve the story being told by revealing the stakes, the history or the identity of the location. Before I even begin sketching, I always ask myself: “What happened here?” This helps me define my initial narrative intent. Every visual choice made is as much about building an atmosphere as it is about solving challenges related to composition, readability, or credibility.

I like to think that my images spark the viewer’s curiosity, inviting them to form their own interpretation of the scene. Through elements like composition, lighting or colour, a simple environment can tell its own story, inviting the viewer to imagine what took place there.

Below, I’ll share some of the key techniques I use daily to bring environments to life with a strong identity and visual storytelling. If you need to update your tools, see our guides to the best best drawing tablets and the best laptops for drawing.

Before I even begin drawing or creating my initial sketches, I always dedicate time to researching all the references needed for my project. I build a library of reference images based on real-world elements such as landscape photographs, architectural details, traditional western paintings, nature, historical documents, animals, objects, etc.

The world around us is an endless source of inspiration! That is also why I enjoy observational drawing and studying my subjects before creating a unique image from my imagination. I might do this using traditional media directly in my sketchbook or digitally; I like to vary my techniques

I always try to give each environment its own distinct personality and identity. It is this identity that guides my artistic choices and shapes every design decision I make after that. An environment that feels like part of a much larger universe is always more impactful and credible.

To achieve this, I always consider architectural elements, the location’s history, culture, climate and technology, along with anything else that helps build a world the viewer wants to explore. The real challenge is successfully turning this environment into a veritable character in its own right within the story.

During my creative process, I often explore silhouettes and shapes before diving into the details. This allows me to focus on the overall forms and define the primary forms. Finding strong, impactful silhouettes, even from a distance, ensures the design is instantly recognisable and readable.

This might take the form of quick sketches of various architectural or natural elements. My goal here is to explore multiple possibilities and generate as many iterations as possible to find an interesting design. The silhouettes need to be expressive and recognisable at a glance.

Light is a powerful compositional tool; it helps convey a clear intent and guides the viewer’s eye. I always strive to craft the lighting to create an interesting focal point within the image. Carefully designed lighting can transform an ordinary setting into a memorable scene that evokes a specific emotion.

I often use light as a narrative element to suggest the time of day, the atmosphere or a particular emotion; I view it as a true emotional language. Strong contrast around the main subject immediately draws the eye. Conversely, softer areas allow the viewer’s gaze to rest.

The design phase is probably the most important, which is why, when I have more complex designs to create, I often proceed with a more precise outline to establish a truly solid foundation. This allows me to resolve any challenges that arise when conceptualising a specific environment or architectural style.

I start by establishing the main shapes, then gradually work in the details. It is a decisive step for the rest of the project as during this stage I determine the function of my various designs. Using this process is common in video games.

To bring my environments to life, I enjoy playing with proportions and varying scales. Pairing small elements with gigantic structures instantly captures the viewer’s attention and lends the image an almost mythological aspect.

This dramatic contrast in scale also allows me to create compositions that reinforce this sense of exploration and travel. These contrasts further amplify the feeling of wonder. I love the idea of the viewer imagining themselves exploring these places, much like they would in a video game, for instance

How to draw convincing buildings using real-world references

After gathering photo references of architectural elements for this world, I begin working on the main masses. 3D can be a great tool for laying out initial, very simple shapes made up of primitives like cubes or cylinders. I model my 3D base using Blender.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Once I’ve blocked in the main shapes, I start drawing over them with more precise line work. This allows me to refine the designs and add small details like decorations, props, vegetation, etc. This line work serves as a solid foundation for moving on to colour.

For the final stage, I focus on colours and textures. I aim to achieve a pleasing colour harmony and bring the buildings to life by adding details that suggest imperfection: signs of wear, dirt and stains, etc. I wanted to depict a peaceful and unique place.

Colours define the mood, but they also convey emotion. I love using vibrant shades and harmonies that evoke a sense of wonder. Nature is my primary source of inspiration, though I also draw from the worlds of Studio Ghibli and the work of great western painters.

I view colour as a tool that lends a unique feel to my images and serves as a key narrative element. Much like light, colour allows me to highlight and draw attention to a crucial element within the image.

When creating an illustration, I always strive to ensure the atmosphere aligns with the emotion or story I wish to convey. I place great importance on crafting a unique atmosphere that transforms the setting into a true protagonist of the story being told.

Mystery is also a powerful narrative device; it is an element I love to incorporate into my images because it allows the viewer’s imagination and interpretation to run free. Lighting, composition, the depth of the various planes and colour harmony all play a role in creating this feeling and bringing it to life.

Over the years, I’ve had the opportunity to experiment with various techniques and acquire a range of skills, allowing me to adapt to different media and graphic styles. In a constantly changing world, adaptability is a valuable asset. I strongly encourage exploring different mediums.

Learning tools like 3D software (specifically Blender) proved to be a real asset early in my career. It’s always a great way to satisfy one’s curiosity and challenge oneself. However, I believe the tool itself shouldn’t become the ultimate goal, as it’s easy to get lost in the process.

A group of 50 used puppets and a fake arch to deliver the point that Americans are against the "Arc de Trump."

WASHINGTON, DC — South of Memorial Circle, within eyeshot of the Lincoln Memorial and John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame, more than 50 protesters gathered yesterday, November 5, to oppose Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch ahead of the National Capital Planning Commission’s (NCPC) final meeting to vote on the project.

Hours after the NCPC approved the arch in an 8–4 vote, a district court judge granted the District of Columbia and Virginia a 14-day restraining order to halt construction.

At the event organized by Third Act DC, an environmental and pro-democracy action group for area residents aged 60 and up, two Virginia Congressional representatives, an Arlington County Board member, and Greg Werkheiser, an attorney with Cultural Heritage Partners, spoke about how the arch would infringe on the architectural and spiritual purpose of the space. He was one of two people associated with lawsuits that the District of Columbia and Virginia, the Arlington County Board, as well as Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian filed against the National Park Service and Department of the Interior in opposition to the arch.

#9180. Artist Sun Xun’s new animated film was made over a decade from thousands of artworks

A scene from Sun Xun's Magic Atlas (2026) Courtesy the artist and π Animation Studio

A phrase cinephiles sometimes use to describe a visually beautiful movie is “every frame a painting”, but that is rarely more true than in Magic Atlas, a feature-length animation film by the Chinese painter Sun Xun, which was awarded a Special Jury Prize at the recently concluded Tokyo International Film Festival.

Sun spent ten years, on and off, working on the film, which he largely self-financed; rather than employ professional animators, he employed hundreds of art students (in one interview, he says 500 over the course of production) to produce individual frames, in a sort of supersized workshop model. Each frame has its own tactile quality, particularly in the sequences made in the unconventional animation medium of woodcut. When a shaft of line streams through a high window, piercing the blackness of an otherwise dark room, you can see the individual carving marks scored into the wood, which across several dozen frames dance and shimmer like the scales of a carp moving through a clear pond.

A scene from Sun Xun's Magic Atlas (2026) Courtesy the artist and π Animation Studio

Magic Atlas is a visual artist’s film, and as a storyteller, Sun thinks like a visual artist, proceeding by association, symbolism and dream logic. The magic atlas of the film’s title is a map to the mystic realms traversed by an explorer in a steampunk flying contraption. After the kaleidoscopic imagery of the film’s opening overture, he spends most of the film in one such world, a coal-mining kingdom called Luocha, where he is imprisoned on the eve of a magic festival. Maps are illegal in Luocha, as are memories. The authoritarian logic of the film is definitely allegorical, but the allegory is hard to pin down; the land’s emperor speaks of forced labour and industrial quotas, in perhaps a Maoist register, but the power behind the throne is an Orwellian cabal of anthropomorphised talking animals, who smoke cigars like colonial lords, and the state’s surveillance protocol is carried out by an army of mosquitos with cameras for heads—a swarm, if not a flock (or Flock).

In a manner similar to Chinese cinema’s emerging mystic-virtuoso Bi Gan, Sun is applying poetic ideas derived from Eastern spirituality about the oneness of all things, the many stories that are all one story. The film opens with a quote from Avatamsaka Sutra invoking “the past, the present, the future lying in the present”, and ends with a lengthy monologue, voiced by Sun himself, delivered by a hieroglyphic eagle. Its ideas about the transmigration of souls are mirrored in the mix of animation styles—the film spends most of its time in Luocha, which is rendered in monumental black-and-white woodcuts and illustrations reminiscent of Rockwell Kent, but also jumps at times to different styles that are each a world in and of themselves.

A scene from Sun Xun's Magic Atlas (2026) Courtesy the artist and π Animation Studio

There are homages to Salvador Dalí and Pieter Bruegel the Elder; a segment in riotous pastels with the Jazz Age voluptuousness of Reginald Marsh and a segment animated in crayon and magic marker by Sun’s Instagram followers during the Covid-19 pandemic; and segments informed by Sun’s own research into different styles of traditional Chinese art, including, he said in a post-screening interview, Dunhuang murals, Song dynasty painting, and multiple styles of calligraphy.

Exhibitions of Magic Atlas materials including woodcuts and concept art have shown at the Times Museum of Guangdong, and additional shows are planned in the United States (where Sun is represented by Sean Kelly Gallery). Sun received initial seed funding from Judith Neilson, the Australian philanthropist and founder of the Asian-focused White Rabbit Gallery, whose current show, up through November 15, includes Magic of Atlas – Luocha: An Infinite Journey, an 8ft-high, 52ft- long, 13-panel woodcut relief depicting images from the story in a scroll that can be stopped and started by the eyes of the viewer passing across the work—a static form of visual narrative that can be traced back to antiquity, long before still and moving images diverged.

#9179. Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Whitney Biennial

Having co-curated the 2024 Biennial, Onli returns to the next edition with Winokur, who founded the American Modern Opera Company.

Meg Onli, an organizer behind some of the Whitney Museum of American Art's signature exhibitions, and Zack Winokur, a performing arts director and co-founder, are the co-curators for the 2028 Whitney Biennial, the museum announced today, November 6.

“Meg is one of the most compelling curatorial voices working today, with an extraordinary ability to champion artists and bring fresh perspectives to the history of American art," Scott Rothkopf, director of the Whitney, said in a statement. "Zack is an equally inventive artistic programmer who has become one of the leading voices of his generation through groundbreaking work across opera, theater, dance, and the visual arts. Their partnership promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial."

The news comes just two months after the 2026 Biennial closed and a month after unionized staff at the museum dodged a full-blown strike ahead of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, a blockbuster retrospective co-curated by Onli. The Whitney union was one of four New York City museum unions under United Auto Workers 2110 — along with the Brooklyn Museum, the American Folk Art Museum, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum — that voted to strike amid drawn-out contract negotiations over low compensation, benefits, and workplace conditions. Hours before the planned strike, unionized staffers ratified their second contract and secured a new wage floor, increased parental and bereavement leave, and stronger safety provisions, among other amendments.

First joining the museum as curator-at-large in 2023, Onli co-curated the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Even Better Than the Real Thing, with Chrissie Iles. That same year, Onli was promoted to Nancy and Fred Poses Curator to lead the Whitney’s painting and sculpture acquisition committee, bringing her previous experience as director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles and associate curator at the Institute of Contemporary Art at the University of Pennsylvania.

“From the Whitney’s early Annuals to its many subsequent iterations, the Biennial has a rich history of reinvention that is already giving us much to think about," Onli said in a statement. "I couldn’t be more excited to explore what the Biennial can be alongside Zack, who is such a dynamic thinker, and to see where our conversations with artists lead."

Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company, an interdisciplinary collective comprised of 17 singers, musicians, dancers, and other performing artists. He also served as artistic director for Little Island on Pier 55 and NYPopsUp, a statewide initiative aimed at opening performing arts spaces after COVID-19.

“I’m honored to be curating the Whitney Biennial with Meg,” Winokur added in a statement. “Our shared desire to center objects and people and the collision between them already echoes our collaboration. It’s that energy that makes the dialogue with her so fun and inspiring."

Dating back to 1932, the Whitney Biennial remains the longest-running survey of American art, with more than 3,600 artists participating in the exhibition to date. The 83rd edition is slated to open in March 2028.

Christmas is coming, which means annoying music in shops, an inevitable lack of snow, and Kim Kardashian charging $148 for the contents of her bathroom drawer.

Kim's 'SKIMS Accessories Advent Calendar' has achieved that rare festive miracle: making a chocolate-based advent calendar look like a sound financial investment. Because what we have here, for a cool $148/£158, is twelve days of tat. Hair ties. Scrunchies. Bobby pins. Keychains. A squishy toy. Something called a 'bra elastic headband'. It's essentially the contents of a lost property box.

Unsurprisingly, the internet is having a field day. A viral TikTok unboxing has attracted tens of millions of views, with its creator becoming visibly more exasperated as each compartment reveals another object you could reasonably expect to find down the back of a sofa, culminating in the grand finale: a furry compact mirror keychain.

It's worth saying that from a branding packaging design perspective, it's almost impressive. It's a nice-looking object with pretty illustrations, and the SKIMS wordmark is striking in a bold, festive red. But there's something beautifully 2026 about taking a handful of mundane objects, putting them in expensive-looking packaging and asking people to cough up the cost of an actual spa day. Like so many of this year's main characters (AI, subscription-based everything, $10 matcha lattes), it's overpriced, overhyped and underwhelming. But unlike AI, that $148 leaving your bank account definitely isn't artificial.

In response to the backlash, SKIMS has emailed customers who purchased the advent calendar: “We wanted to reach out personally about your recent purchase of the Holiday 2026 advent calendar. We understand the product did not meet customers’ expectations, and we are truly sorry. We want every customer to be happy with what they receive, and we fell short this time.”

Believe it or not, this isn't the first time we've seen a celebrity's brand take a hit as a result of an underwhelming advent calendar. Back in 2017, popular vlogger Zoella faced backlash for her own calendar. Like Kim's it contained only twelve doors, all of which were filled with items that might be found down the back of a sofa. Unlike Kim's, it was a mere $60. Inflation, eh?

If you need help restoring your faith in the festive season, check out the magical Disney Holiday Short, which is moving people to tears.

#9177. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.
