You're flying it because 90,000 points delivering $8,000–$12,000 in value is one of the most efficient uses of a points balance available anywhere in loyalty programs today.

For the ChooseFI traveler who has optimized their earning strategy and is ready to deploy a meaningful points balance on a once-in-a-decade trip, this is one of the most compelling redemptions on the board.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

The Cricut Maker 4 Creative Pro bundle has £245 off.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Although the craft machine manufacturer's own sale hasn't started yet, Cricut Black Friday deals are starting to come in at other sellers, and there's a tempting bundle offer at Very. The UK retailer has £245 off a huge Cricut Maker 4 bundle, which is reduced from £647.77 to £399.49.

The package includes a wide range of tools and materials and even Cricut's BrightPad Go lightbox. It's a big saving, but how does it compare now that Cricut has released the Maker 5, which has a slightly lower starting price? It's worth comparing the bundles available for each as both are among the best Cricut machines you can get.

This big bundle deal includes the Cricut Maker 4 machine with installed Fine-Point Blade, Light Grip Machine Mat, Fine Point Pen, several weeders, Scoring Stylus, Scraper and Spatula, plus six smart iron-on sheers, transfer tape and a range of permanent and removable Smart Vinyl. You also get the Cricut BrightPad Go lightbox, which normally costs £100 alone and doesn't tend to be included in bundles.

For comparison, the Maker 5 direct from Cricut with the smaller Essentials Bundle costs the same price. This bundle contains the machine and installed Fine Point Cutting Tool with a Scoring Tool, Engraving Tool, Dual-Sided Marker, Light Grip Machine Mat and a smaller range of materials to get started with.

The Ultimate Plus bundle deal, which Cricut says is worth £594, adds a Deep Cutting Tool, Rotary Blade + Housing, Knife Blade + Housing, the Cricut Easy Press Mini LT, Portable Trimmer Weeder, Scraper and Spatula Reverse Tweezers, Markers and a lot more materials.

At this price, yes, I'd still consider the Cricut Maker 4. The Maker 5 was released just two months ago, and it does have a couple of advantages, but the difference in capability and performance is very small. After all, the Maker 4 isn't yet two years old.

One advantage of the Maker 5 is that it has 25% more carriage clearance, allowing it to cut and engrave approved materials up to 3mm thick (compared to 2.4 mm on the Maker 4). It's also around a third smaller in size and nearly 2kg lighter than the Maker 4. It has an open-top design instead of the traditional flip-up lid and introduces a new snap-in Universal Pen holder and an integrated cutting tool housing, whereas the Maker 4 uses a classic Clamp A and Clamp B setup.

However, both machines have the same maximum cutting speed of up to 14.1 inches per second, and the same materials are compatible with both, so there's no issue of the newer Maker being more future proof. The smaller, lighter Maker 5 might be more convenient for smaller desks, easy stowing or travel, but if the size factor isn't a deal breaker for you, Very's Black Friday deal on the older machine may be tempting, allowing you to get started with more tools and materials.

See our full Cricut Maker 5 review and Cricut Maker 4 review for more details on each. For something more compact and travel-friendly, consider the Cricut Joy 2.

#9155. Is Sexy Art Back, or Is It Just Me?

From Willem de Kooning’s miserable nudes to Alexandra Barth’s hot and bothered architecture, sex is in the air in Chicago.

CHICAGO — I see a lot of exhibitions in Chicago, and lately, I have been noticing more than a few that feel almost ridiculously erotic. I mean, I get it, there's always been plenty of eros in art, but I haven't observed it much lately at the school where I teach nor in the shows that I view. Is sex back? Or it could just be me. I turned 50 this past year, and popular culture suggests that this might be what happens around my age, à la Sharon Horgan's Youth and Olivia Colman's Wicker, both recent screen-based explorations of lusty midlife ladyhood.

For those who have never had one or maybe never will, female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100. It is not an easy ride. Shifting from one state to the other causes severe whiplash for driver and passengers alike. That’s based on an admittedly minuscule survey, though fear not, this will not be a personal essay about my own sexuality or that of my acquaintances. God, no. Maybe after everyone’s dead. What proceeds, instead, is a round-up of exhibitions that, for me, have a strong connecting thread, obviously red, and not discussed much if at all in the various associated didactics.

What shows? Last spring, Alice Tippit’s sly, meticulous paintings at the DePaul Art Museum had me thinking I probably needed to start talking to a therapist again, because what was going on in my head was not articulated anywhere in the otherwise delightful catalogue. Not even close. During the summer, SHADOW at tête-à-tête-à-tête, a wicked little curatorial project of Shannon Stratton, included Holly Murkerson’s sensuous photographs of a stone passageway worth entering and two dark leather-and-wood stools by David Sprecher and Neiva Mulhearn that required straddling and peering into.

What wasn’t a turn-on was the Art Institute of Chicago’s summer blockbuster, Willem de Kooning Drawing. You wouldn’t know from the glowing reviews or polite museum text that miserable naked women filled the walls. I like a good nude as much as anyone, but at some point, maybe it was the third room — definitely by the time I got to the giant rowboat charcoals of the mid-60s — de Kooning’s subjects started to look like crime victims.

Left: Lee Miller, “Woman with Hand on Head” (also known as “Coiffure”) (1931), photograph; right: Lee Miller, “Charlie Chaplin with chandelier" (1932), photograph (both photos courtesy Art Institute of Chicago)

#9154. Getty Pitches In on First-Ever Conservation of an Earthquake-Damaged 17th-Century Church in the Andean Highlands of Peru

The Getty will work with local authorities on the first-ever conservation project on a 17th-century earthen church in the Andean highlands of the Cusco region of Peru. The Church of Santo Tomás de Aquino, locally known as the Church of Rondocan, is a sacred cultural heritage site. Over the years, earthquakes have damaged the church, and not only the structure but also the church’s collection of more than 300 cultural objects is under threat.

The Peruvian government has allotted $5 million to a multi-year initiative that will strengthen the earthen site and support the conservation and care of both building and collection, which includes 17th- and 18th-century paintings, gilded wooden retablos and associated sculptures, ecclesiastical textiles, and more. The Getty will contribute expertise from staffers across various departments. Related Articles Collective Climate Action Implemented by Los Angeles Arts Institutions New Research Suggests Peru's Mysterious 'Band of Holes' May Have Been an Ancient Marketplace

In a Baroque style and with thick adobe brick walls, the church, Getty says, is one of many remote earthen sacred sites that have gone without regular maintenance while suffering damage from earthquakes. The Getty Conservation Institute’s Seismic Retrofitting Project (SRP) employs high-tech analytical techniques to strengthen earthen heritage sites against quakes and create long-term plans to monitor and maintain them. A regional office of the Ministry of Culture of Peru will work in partnership with SRP to develop a comprehensive conservation and seismic retrofitting project, with construction to begin in 2027.

“Since 2011, the Conservation Institute has worked across Peru with local conservation professionals to conserve some of the country’s most significant earthen architectural buildings,” said Claudia Cancino, principal project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute, and project lead for the Sacred Heritage in the Andes Project, in press materials. “These are the buildings in which so much of daily life in these regions takes place, but they require specialized efforts for their protection. With this collective effort, we will be able to provide expertise and support for the Rondocan community, who have been the primary caretakers of the church and its incredible collections for generations.”

Among the most notable works in the collection is a series of eight large easel paintings by the Italian Jesuit priest and painter Bernardo Bitti (1548–1610), “Principales Misterios de la Vida y Muerte de Cristo Nuestro Salvador y de la Virgen Santísima” (“Principal Mysteries of the Life and Death of Christ our Savior and the Holy Virgin Mary”), painted in Cusco, likely in the later 1590s. When Getty staffers visited the church in 2010, they were surprised to find the works, thought at the time by most art historians to be lost. One painting from the series, La Oración en el huerto (“Prayer in the Garden”), will be transferred to the Getty in 2027 to undergo scientific analysis and conservation treatment.

Per Britannica, Bitti is credited with introducing Mannerism to Peruvian art after training in Rome as an artist and then becoming a Jesuit. He went to Cusco in 1583, remaining there for a year, constructing the high altar of the Jesuit church. His travels in Juli, La Paz, and Lima, as well as numerous visits to Cusco, positioned him as an influence on painters throughout the Andes.

“What makes the church’s collection unique, beyond its richness for such an isolated church, is that no evidence suggests it has ever been restored,” said Stéphanie Auffret, senior project specialist at the Getty Conservation Institute, in press materials. “As such, it represents a rare opportunity to document the artifacts, generating knowledge useful to a variety of stakeholders. The study of the decorative surfaces of the lateral altarpieces, for instance, with their rarely preserved original materials, will inform the interpretation of similar decorative surfaces in other churches in Peru.”

The work involves objects that are in regular use, added Auffret: “This project also provides a wonderful opportunity to interact with the local community, who care deeply about the site and all its cultural objects, such as the sculptures they carry as part of processions during the Semana Santa. Preserving a collection in use presents challenges as well as valuable exchanges with community members, something not experienced in a museum’s context.”

#9153. Clouds Were Once Photography’s Greatest Challenge

The Met Museum’s “Chasing Clouds” is a pleasing romp through the technical problem of capturing clouds at photography’s beginning.

The original 1996 Windows XP default background is arguably the most viewed photo of all time; its cumulus puffs drifting across a way-too-blue sky are seared into my and countless others’ Y2K childhoods. Such images of fluffy clouds are so ubiquitous that it’s hard to believe they once presented one of photography’s greatest technological challenges. The Met exhibition Chasing Clouds is a pleasing romp through the history of this problem through a union of art and science, spanning the early 1800s to 1929 — roughly photography’s first century. While the medium showed promise as “the pencil of nature,” its first processes were overly sensitive to blue light, registering the sky as a blank white space, impossibly overexposed.

While this lent some images a minimalist mystique, like John Beasley Greene’s “The Nile in Front of the Theban Hills” (1853–54), other photographers resorted to painting clouds into their landscapes by hand. An initial breakthrough came when French photographer Gustave Le Gray figured out how to stitch together two pictures — one calibrated to sky, and the other to land and sea. (Photographic fakery is as old as the medium itself.)

Though the exhibition begins with painted cloud studies and ends with photographic modernism, visual discoveries unfold in a dialogue between painting and technology rather than as a scientific march from one to the other. This makes for a much more interesting story; obsolescence is often a capitalist public relations trick.

Noble Audio's Astrid have a triple-driver system and sleek looks .

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Noble Audio has had one seriously busy year in 2026, and it's not over yet. The Texas-based company has impressed us with in-ear monitors and over-ear cans alike, from the Lu Ban wired IEMs made from cocobolo wood to the Noble FoKus Artemis over-ear ANC headphones, which we gave a near-perfect 4.5-star review.

Now, it's adding another wireless in-ear headphone to its lineup. The Astrid will sit somewhere in the middle of its current offering, so they won't enter our pick of the best budget IEMs, but they offer an intriguing proposition: three driver technologies for the ability to both adapt sound to your own unique hearing profile and adjust it to how you want it to sound.

They look sharp too with an intricate silver-toned frost-like pattern over the glass fiber earbud and the charging case.

Hybrid earphones are a familiar territory for Noble Audio, which has explored driver combinations in its universal and custom in-ear monitors. Astrid brings that experience to a new wireless design.

There are three driver technologies in each ear piece: an 8.3mm dynamic driver, 6mm planar driver and a balanced armature. The first uses a PU diaphragm with an aluminium-magnesium alloy dome. This works alongside the other two technologies in a hybrid system that takes account of differences between your left and right ears as well as the way your hearing differs from other people’s.

Using Audiodo Personal Sound, a short test checks each ear and creates a personal hearing profile. This is then used to adjust playback to your ears. Meanwhile, the Audiodo Equalizer allows you to adjust bass, mids and treble as preferred: the result is sound that accounts for both how you hear and how you like your music to sound, the company says.

The new TWS has Active Noise Cancellation and a Transparency mode to let through outside sound when needed. Microphone noise and wind reduction are intended to help with calls, while Bluetooth 6.0 and two-device multipoint make it possible to keep a phone and laptop connected at the same time.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Noble cites up to 11 hours of listening per charge and up to 40 hours including the case, depending on settings, with USB-C and wireless charging. There's a choice of silicone ear tips, and the buds have IPX4 splash resistance.

Priced at $539 / £499, the Astrid sits above the $200 Osprey and the Rex5 but below the flagship Prestige Encore II in Noble's growing TWS range. You can order at nobleaudio.com and selected retailers.

#9151. Aros museum in Aarhus, Denmark acquires sun-like Olafur Eliasson sculpture in new partnership with the artist

Olafur Eliasson's Presence (2025), installed at the Queensland Art Gallery and Gallery of Modern Art in Brisbane

Photo: Chloë Callistemon © QAGOMA Courtesy of the artist; neugerriemschneider, Berlin; and Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York © 2025 Olafur Eliasson

The Aros Aarhus Art Museum in eastern Denmark will acquire a major piece by the high-profile Danish-Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson—a crowd-pleasing vast glowing yellow sphere that appears to hover in space (Presence, 2025)—as part of a new long-term partnership.

The initiative between the artist and the museum, called “Shared Futures”, also encompasses Thin Ice, a solo exhibition to open autumn 2027. “This exhibition presents key works from recent decades alongside new projects reflecting Eliasson’s growing engagement with the climate, ecology, and humanity’s relationship with its surroundings,” says a statement.

A new site-specific version of Eliasson’s installation Waterfall (2004) will meanwhile be installed on Aros’s Art Square from 9 October next year; Studio Olafur Eliasson will also create a publicly accessible library collection of books on Eliasson’s artistic production at Aros under the plans. In addition, the partnership includes a dedicated postdoctoral research position in collaboration with Aarhus University.

Eliasson's Waterfall (2019), installed at Tate Modern in London

Photo: Anders Sune Berg; Courtesy of the artist; neugerriemschneider, Berlin; Tanya Bonakdar Gallery, New York © 2019 Olafur Eliasson

Eliasson says in a statement: “Aros has supported my work in Denmark for many years, so it felt natural to make my online archive and library available there… the ambition is to show that museums can offer depth and focus for engaging with an artist’s practice in a more detailed, granular way.” The museum is also home to Eliasson’s rainbow rooftop walkway Your Rainbow Panorama (2011).

Eliasson's Your rainbow panorama (2011) at Aros

Tina Sørensen © Schmidt Hammer Lassen, 2026

Rebecca Matthews, the museum's director, tells The Art Newspaper: “I first met Olafur Eliasson when I was chief executive of the European Capital of Culture in 2017, when he created an extraordinary stage design for the performance Tree of Codes. We were supposed to have our photograph taken together, but it was pouring with rain, so we ended up standing in a colonnade, talking. I remember thinking: If I ever get to lead a museum, he will be the first person I call.” Matthews became director of Aros in 2022.

In December 2025, Eliasson appeared on The Art Newspaper podcast A brush with…. with Ben Luke. “His works can be deceptively simple or enormously complex, but often share a rigorous and reductive geometry, which may conversely produce expansive and multifarious perceptual, sensory and embodied effects,” wrote Luke.

Site-specific installation called Life opened this week at the Fondation Beyeler near Basel in Switzerland and can be visited at all hours

#9150. Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallegic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).

When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.

That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives, you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?

Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”

MC: And my editor was like, “Yeah, you can't do that. No one's gonna want to read a book that you wrote simply for money.” But I also knew that this was a commercial idea, and that did inform it. I have been quite shameless about the fact that I want my work to reach a wide audience. That has always, always mattered to me. It was the beginning of the pandemic, and part of the way that I pitched it was this idea that there's gonna be a big financial crisis and the dynamics are more nuanced than simply talking about the one percent. There's this idea of a coming economic collapse or a coming financial crisis. But as soon as we're in it, it's not this cyclical model. The crisis is the system that we're in that is so broken.

H: That gradation of class that usually doesn't get talked about is such a crucial contribution of this book. What led you to stratify these stories based on subcategories that often just get collapsed into “working class, middle class, upper class”?

MC: Class is really informative about who I am and how I move through the world and my relationships. And I felt like it was really, really lacking in our discourse. I feel a bit hesitant to use the word “discourse,” but it's just true. And it's not just about discourse, it's more mundane than that. It's the way that someone like me can say, “I'm an Arab, cis, heterosexual woman,” with total ease, but class doesn't really come into it. There's a dishonesty there. Actually, class is really, really important. And many of us aren't really talking about that in accurate and fruitful ways.

#9149. Moab Petroglyphs Discovered Vandalized: ‘Irreplaceable Cultural Resources’

The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Utah is seeking the culprits behind two incidents of vandalism that left protected petroglyphs near Moab riddled with crude carvings, including that signature and another, less distinct marking.

The vandals reportedly struck one site along Highway 279, a scenic stretch parallel to the Colorado River, and one by Hell’s Revenge, a well-known off-road slickrock trail. Photos taken by the Bureau, and first published by SF Gate, show clear damage to the petroglyphs that decorate the rock fave: In one photo, an investigator is seen measuring huge letters—spelling “Craig W”—that now cover a portion of petroglyph depicting animals. Related Articles See the Official Trailer for "Dig," Amy Pohler and Michael Schur's New Comedy Series 2,500-Year-Old Mesoamerican Observatory Discovered in Sierra Norte Mountains of Mexico

Writing on social media, the BLM described the petroglyph as “irreplaceable cultural resources” which are protected under the Archaeological Resources Protection Act.

“Our cultural resources are part of our shared heritage,” the Bureau said. “Once damaged, they cannot be restored to their original condition. We ask visitors to respect these resources and help protect them for future generations.”

Petroglyphs near Moab and beyond are a frequent target for criminal mischief and looting, amid more existential threats posed by recent government rollbacks of their protections. In 2021, a series of sacred, 300-year petroglyphs along the cliffs of Hawaii were defaced with a paintball gun, marking one in a string of incidents involving the artworks. A group of petroglyphs located at the Volcanic Tableland in Bishop, California, carved into the rock by the Paiute-Shoshone before European colonization, have faced multiple episodes of vandalism, including desecration and even theft: Criminals reportedly used power saws to remove large sections of rock featuring the carvings. The BLM managed to recover the stolen petroglyph, though the suspects remained at large.

Whoever they are, they’ll find little mercy from locals. “The minimum sentence for this crime should be life without parole,” wrote one user on the r/California subreddit at the time. “If you disrespect historical artifacts of great significance you should be labeled an enemy of the public. Zero tolerance.”

#9148. Mona Chalabi on Money and Art

An interview with the Pulitzer Prize winner, Lori Waxman on bringing sexy back in Chicago, stolen Picasso prints found, and the problem with clouds.

“I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it,” Mona Chalabi says in her new book Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are — or tried to, anyway, before her editor stopped her. The Iraqi-British, Pulitzer-winning artist and illustrator has made a career saying what nobody else can, or will — calling out fellow journalists for their refusal to report on Palestine, for instance. Today, she talks to Associate Editor Laskhmi Rivera Amin about her data-driven, hand-drawn process, as well as how class and inequality shape journalism, art, and our lives.

Funny — as an editor, my favorite thing is not stopping my writers. That’s precisely how Lori Waxman’s piece on the return of sexy art in Chicago was born. No, this is not a personal essay about her or her acquaintances’ sexuality (“Maybe after everyone’s dead,” she says). It’s much better — loaded with art historical judgments (has anyone referred to Willem de Kooning’s drawings as “slasher sketches” before? We ought to); discussion of glory holes and sexy architecture; and gems about life (“female middle-age libido sets at either zero or 1,000, on a scale of one to 100”). God, I love my job.

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. #9147. Collectors Jill and Peter Kraus Want Artists to Look at Their Upstate New York Property and React to It

On Jill and Peter Kraus’s almost 400-acre property in Dutchess County, New York, the rolling hills add to the serenity and also create drama. Standing in front of any one of the 18 commissioned outdoor sculptures here, you can’t see any of the others. Sabine Hornig’s 2010 concrete work, Entrance With Floating Stairs II, for example, stands atop a hill. “What I love about this piece is the siting of it,” Jill Kraus told me as we pulled up to the work on a Polaris utility terrain vehicle this past May. “You come across it, and as you drive toward it, it starts to disappear—and then it comes back. I think this is the most perfectly sited piece we have. Everybody thinks we manipulated the landscape here—we did not.” Related Articles A New Hudson Valley Art Space Promises to Be As Accessible as It Is In Flux Leah Ke Yi Zheng Joins Antenna Space, Pérez Art Museum Miami to Honor Nicolas Berggruen, and More: Industry Moves for October 28, 2026

For the past two decades, the Krauses have worked with artists to conceive of site-specific artworks for the expansive property. “Most people who collect outdoor sculpture just buy and plop it—they have ‘plop art,’” Jill said. “People are surprised when they come here because they think that’s what we’ve done. They’re always shocked at how we work.”

To see all of the outdoor commissions, from a Roxy Paine tree to a set of colorful abstract sculptures by Franz West, plus the Art Barn, which is like a mini museum, requires about six hours, with at least two of those having to be well past dusk to accommodate three video projection pieces. The works differ greatly in scale, materials, and approach, but the connective tissue between them all, Jill said, is “they’re all dealing with this place.”

The tour typically begins with Sol LeWitt’s Dome Structure (Four Domes and A Sphere), his only spherical work ever realized. The concrete sculpture, which stands atop a 10-foot foundation so it doesn’t slide down the hill, holds a tender spot for the Krauses, whose children were friends with LeWitt’s children at boarding school; the couple asked the artist to make them a work before his death in 2007. In the two decades since, the piece has weathered the elements, though not without fissures.

When commissioning an artist to make a new work, Jill opts for a collaborative approach, which she attributed to having gone to art school for both her BFA and MFA, and working as a design director for 20 years. “I like to discuss ideas and push artists out of their comfort zone to get them to think about things that they might not normally think about,” she said. “We want them to look at the natural habitat and then react to it.” The couple doesn’t work with an adviser, and instead sources any engineers or fabricators needed to realize a project themselves. “It’s all about talking things through. We work through ideas, and I think that’s what makes what we’re doing very different from what most other collectors do.”

Their one requirement is that an artist visit at least twice, “once when the leaves are on the trees, and once when the leaves are off the trees,” Jill said. “Then we say to them, ‘You can drive all over the property. We’ll show you every square inch, and you find a spot where you want to work.’”

One of the Krauses’ most collaborative pieces is Between sky and earth by Tatiana Trouvé, which was first commissioned in 2012 and has been adjusted at least yearly ever since. “I warned them that it was going to take time, and that this slowness was part of my work,” Trouvé told me. “They said, ‘We have all the time in the world!’”

The work imagines the Guardian, a hermit who lives atop a wooded mound about 65 feet in diameter, situated in a clearing on the property. He’s not in at the moment, but you can peruse his belongings—books, chairs, a patent leather shoe, suitcases, blankets, a rolled-up cot, paint cans, a collection of ropes—all fabricated in concrete, copper, or bronze. The work is in a constant state of flux, in dialogue with its natural environs and the seasons. “We’re trying to decide, how much do we let nature take over the piece?” Jill said, noting that moss has begun to grow over parts of it, while some elements have had to be moved after proving too heavy for the branches they once hung from. “It’s not an object,” Jill added. “It’s a world.”

“Jill and Peter have that touch of madness that belongs only to passionate people driven by their deep love for artworks and artists,” Trouvé said. “Alongside art and artists, they live an adventure built on sincerity, audacity, and determination.”

The Krauses started collecting art in 1980, their first purchase being a print by Pierre Alechinsky, a birthday present for Jill, shortly after they married. Works on paper would be their focus for the next several years because that was all they could afford at the time. “What we really liked was sculpture, but that’s hard to collect when you live in a New York City apartment,” Jill said. They put off buying a summer home for a few decades until finally they decided that if they bought a substantial piece of land, they could commission artists to make site-responsive sculptures there. They began searching within a two-hour radius of Manhattan, at first thinking that Connecticut might be right.

“What we didn’t realize is that the difference in the geography from Connecticut to New York is huge,” she said. “A glacier came down the Hudson River Valley and took the tops off the mountains, so everything is rolling hills on the New York side. The Connecticut side is very tight, peak to valley, so there are no big, expansive views. The difference visually is huge.” In 2001, their broker recommended they see a piece of land that wasn’t on the market, with rolling hills where the previous owner, actor James Cagney, grazed his long-horned cattle. “We came to look at it, and we said, ‘Absolutely, this is it,’” Jill recalled.

The Krauses are unlike their neighbors, many of whom own this much land so they can ride horses or hunt. After buying the property, when asked if they were interested in either of those, Jill replied with a twist on agriculture: “No, we’re growing art.” Their modestly scaled modernist house, nestled in a secluded spot, is also an anomaly up here: They were able to persuade the Dutchess Land Conservancy that such a structure had “historical precedent”—a requirement of their purchase agreement—because Harvard Five architects John M. Johansen and Marcel Breuer both had connections to the area.

The brightly colored walls in the home are filled with the Krauses’ collection, including works by Tacita Dean, Raymond Saunders, Rachel Harrison, Richard Tuttle, Rudolf Stingel, and Franz Ackermann, the latter a commission. Upstairs is To Count: Intransitive (1972/2009), a site-specific piece by Mel Bochner, who inscribed 10 windows with hundreds of numbers, starting with 0, in different arrangements. In the late afternoon, the setting sun sends their shadows onto the floor and walls.

On the other side of the property is the Art Barn, which holds a rotating display of artworks. When I visited, there were pieces by Meriem Bennani, Alvaro Barrington, Lauren Halsey, and Helen Marten on view. In one corner was Ericka Beckman’s mesmerizing video Cinderella (1986), with an original set piece installed nearby; around another corner was Alex Da Corte’s video Rubber Pencil Devil (2018), which they saw when it debuted at the Carnegie International that year. “When it was time to install it, I said, ‘I can’t put this in a white box—it won’t work,’” Jill recalled. Peter suggested calling the artist for his thoughts, to which Jill replied, “I’d rather ask for forgiveness than for permission.” She painted the walls yellow to match the playful spirit of the work and added her colorful dining chairs.

If there is one thing that characterizes the Krauses’ approach to collecting, it is the sheer investment of time. Due to a tricky structural issue, their home took eight years to complete; but that’s nothing compared to the outdoor sculptures. Matthew Monahan’s Second Nature (2023) took around 14 years, though the first eight or so of those involved the Krauses trying to convince the artist to take on the commission. It’s not unusual for that stage to take some time; for example, at the moment, they are in the ideation process with Max Hooper Schneider and Meriem Bennani. “Jill and Peter are aware of the conventional solutions that artists use to get the job done,” Monahan told me by email, “and I suspect they work to positively sabotage these conventions by selecting artists with little or no experience in outdoor work, and by insisting on site specificity.”

Monahan was intrigued by the Krauses’ aversion to “plop art.” “They invited me to pick the site. There was no deadline and no discussion of cost,” he said. He spent several months considering where he would place his piece, ultimately choosing one area, only to find out that Trouvé had already gotten dibs on it. He then submitted a proposal for a plot of land about 200 yards from the main house, but on a subsequent visit, Peter drove him out to yet another site, one with a slope, hoping that Monahan would agree to that instead.

Alongside Peter, Monahan began to rethink the modeling of his sculpture, with artist and patron determining the distance and grade of the slope by walking away from each other. The resulting artwork is double the size of Monahan’s original model: a 6-foot-high, 50-foot-long wall, the front half mostly buried in the ground, the back half topped off with a 6-foot-tall sculpture of a figure that has been cut up and then welded back together. The wall, constructed to resemble chicken wire, has been filled with rocks from the property as well as other remnants of the figure (a hand here, half a nose there). A true sculpture in the round, the work shifts as you circle it: A black metal screen bisects the wall, hiding the site’s slope and its dwarfing scale when seen from downhill.

“The sloping site made the work better, [creating] a dynamic viewing experience that has to be walked through [and] around, so that at one end the viewer is standing face-to-face with the figures, and at the other end, the figures stand high above them,” Monahan said. He sees the Krauses as “friends and collaborators,” adding that “the years were not spent on aspiring to vertical grandeur but on a complex, layered negotiation with each other and nature.”

Negotiating with nature is a hallmark of the works the Krauses have commissioned. Michael Van Valkenburgh, the property’s landscape architect, introduced the Krauses to a student of his, Jon Piasecki, in Harvard’s Graduate School of Design. On Piasecki’s first visit to the property, he ran into a forested area and called out that he’d found the remnants of an old stone wall, assembled haphazardly back when farmers cleared the field. He told Peter that he wanted to build a path along the wall. Soon, using stones from nearby Connecticut, Piasecki began laying out the almost unnoticeable pathway—beginning atop the wall, continuing inside the wall, emerging atop the wall—in the Fibonacci sequence. Working with only a hammer and chisel, he spent three years, from April to November, on the project, finishing in 2009. “Everything here is placed here for a reason,” Jill said. “At one point, I was walking through while he was working, and I said, ‘Look, a snail.’ And he replied, ‘I know. I put it there.’”

Further along in the woods is a Jose Dávila sculpture fabricated to look like cut-out sections of a blue shipping container—“a riff on if a Donald Judd stack had fallen over,” Jill joked. Beyond that is a labyrinth-like installation of mirrors by Jeppe Hein that reflects the forest back onto itself. In a nearby field is a series of sculptures by Katja Strunz that imagines the spreading of a mother dandelion’s seeds. A towering piece by Monika Sosnowska is, as Jill put it, “a staircase that has collapsed and has become a tree in the forest.”

After dusk, Jill took me to see the three video installations. The late Ján Mančuška’s short film The Invisible Exists (2009) was his only animation work, an enigmatic story rendered in ballpoint pen. Tony Oursler’s installation, titled +/- (2023), sends three projections onto different tree lines and relays an idiosyncratic history of the Hudson River Valley, where the artist grew up, bringing in everything from technological advances like the telegraph and early filmmaking to references to West Point, IBM, and the cultish religion of the Oneida Community.

But the tour de force is Doug Aitken’s Lighthouse (2012). Aitken visited before the house was built. “It really struck me—the power of the landscape,” Aitken told me, recalling that he told the Krauses, “If you ever do build something here, I think we should make an artwork that makes it disappear, because this impression that we’re having today is so profound.”

Aitken visited several times over the course of a year—in all four seasons and at all hours of the day—to capture video footage of the natural landscape. Lighthouse projects those images onto the house. “We found all these moments of the changing entropy of the landscape: the melting snow, the sun moving across the forest,” the artist said. In the resulting piece, “as day turns into night, the structure turns into this image of the landscape around it.”

“It was profound finding collaborators who were willing to take that journey,” Aitken said. “As far as collectors go, it’s so important to see things beyond the [object], and instead look to actually push where art can go, what it can be, and what forms it can transform into. They really believe in the true potential of art—the idea of art as an agent of change. They’re open to challenging works, provocative ideas, and works that are outside the box. We need more of that.”

For fans of the tiny tablet, this is a worthy upgrade.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For what feels like the first time in years, Apple is in experimenting mode. From folding iPhones to touchscreen MacBooks, the company is suddenly dropping innovative products rather than incremental upgrades. But while the new iPad mini might not be the most exciting new release of 2026, for a select group of users, it might just be the best iPad yet.

The 8th generation iPad mini upgrades almost everything about the tiny tablet. The headline feature has to be the OLED display, which is brighter, crisper and more vibrant than any iPad mini display we've seen. Meanwhile, minor design changes have resulted in a thinner and lighter body – which is a much more meaningful change than it might sound.

I've always been a fan of the iPad mini. Sure, larger models like the Pro feature M-series chips and ProMotion displays, but sometimes there's no replacement for portability. As the famous saying goes, 'your best iPad is the one you have with you' – and being able to sling the iPad mini into a tote bag is invaluable. And the first thing I noticed when picking it up was the reduction in size. At 5.4mm thick and 255 grams, it's just ridiculously thin and light.

And the second thing I noticed was, yes, that OLED display. While it isn't quite as stunning as the new MacBook Pro's PROLED XDR display, those bright colours and inky blacks look stunning. For creatives, a bright, colour-accurate screen is a must, and now the smallest iPad delivers one in spades.

But there is a glaring omission. In this day and age, a 60hz refresh rate feels slow and stuttering on any device, let alone one that starts at £699. Apple's 120hz ProMotion display has made its way to most of its products by now, but it's surprising, given the scale of the rest of the updates (and the price increase) that the iPad mini hasn't been blessed with one. Reddit, as you might imagine, has not been kind.

But if you can put aside the lack of ProMotion, there's so much to love here. Performance-wise, that A20 Pro chip (which also resides in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo) is incredibly speedy and efficient – I'm managing to eke out around ten hours on a single charge.

Another improvement is the sound quality. Apple has somehow managed to place the speakers underneath the display (or as Apple calls it, the 'acoustic display'), and the result is powerfully punchy audio for a tablet so small.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Overall, if you're somebody who already loves the iPad mini and has the cash to burn for an upgrade, the 8th generation model is a winner. Every improvement adds up to a meaningfully enhanced experience, particularly the OLED screen and the weight loss. Now, if Apple could just bring itself to give us a 120hz display, the 9th generation iPad mini might just be the perfect tiny tablet.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

#9145. The Most Expensive Artworks by Pablo Picasso Ever Sold at Auction

Over the course of seven decades, Pablo Picasso maintained prolific periods of artistic output that cemented his status as the one of most coveted artists of all time. The modernist’s most prized paintings derive from various stages in his life: the early-career Rose and Blue periods and his groundbreaking experiments in Cubism, through his output in the years leading up to and during World War II up to the late 1960s, when he was already world famous.

Central to Picasso’s oeuvre are portraits of his various muses: Marie-Thérèse Walter, Dora Maar, Françoise Gilot, and Jacqueline Roque, each of whom the artist had a series of complicated affairs. These portraits, which range from sensual to tormented, have become some of the most recognizable in art history.

In the years since his death in 1973, Picasso’s stature as an artist elevated to the highest ranks, with some of his works going for more than $100 million in public auctions and reportedly at even higher sums in private deals. Currently, he remains the top-grossing artist at auction worldwide, raking in $245 million across 3,400 lots in 2020 alone. “He is in many ways the gold standard of the art market,” said dealer Larry Gagosian in an interview with ARTnews. “I think he’ll remain that way for the foreseeable future.” Below, a look at the top auction sales of works by the Spanish master.

Femme assise depicts French artist and model Fernande Olivier, who went with Picasso to a remote village in Spain during the summer of 1909. While there, she posed for a number of paintings. One of the few early Picasso Cubist works still in private hands, Femme assise sold for £43.2 million ($63.4 million) at a Sotheby’s London evening sale in 2016, where it exceeded the $43.1 million presale estimate. A telephone bidder won the painting, which had remained under the same roof for four decades. The anonymous seller had bought it in 1973 at Sotheby’s for £340,000 ($486,000). With many of Picasso’s early Cubist works in museum collections, Femme assise was a rarity on the open market at the time. “There hasn’t been a painting of this importance at auction in potentially a generation,” Helena Newman, Sotheby’s head of Impressionist and modern art in London, said at the time.

This vibrant red portrait of Dora Maar measures only 25⅝ by 21¼ inches. Auctioned by Christie’s New York in May 2015 at the house’s “Looking Forward to the Past” sale, it went for $67.4 million to an anonymous buyer, surpassing its $55 million high estimate.

Consigned by Las Vegas casino mogul and top collector Steve Wynn, the work was the third-highest sale of the night, which also saw the record-setting sale of Picasso’s Delacroix-inspired Les femmes d’Alger Version “O” for $179.4 million (see below). Before Buste de femme was acquired by Wynn, it had passed through the hands of the artist’s granddaughter Marina Picasso and Geneva modern art dealer Jan Krugier.

Bearing a second painting on the reverse, the rare double-sided canvas La gommeuse was painted by Picasso when he was only 19 years old. The artist created the picture while grieving the death of his friend and fellow artist Carles Casagemas, who had recently died by suicide—a tragedy that ushered in the Blue Period.

The work sold for $67.45 million (including buyer’s premium) at Sotheby’s New York in November 2015, though it was hammered in below its presale estimate of $60 million. The painting’s seller, American billionaire Bill Koch, had purchased it for $3 million in 1984 at auction. It wasn’t until 2000, while the work was being conserved, that a hidden portrait mocking Picasso’s friend and patron Pere Mañach was discovered on the reverse.

Before Koch owned it, La gommeuse had passed through the hands of esteemed French art dealer Ambroise Vollard, New York dealer Lucien Demotte, and Austrian-American film director Josef von Sternberg, who bought it in 1935 and sold it in 1949 at Sotheby’s for $3,600.

Picasso created his famed Guernica and The Weeping Woman in 1937 amid the tumultuous years of the Spanish Civil War. Painted the same year, Femme au béret et à la robe quadrillée features a more joyous image, that of his muse Marie-Thérèse Walter in a blue, red, and white outfit set against a purple background.

The painting made its auction debut during a Sotheby’s Impressionist and modern art sale in London. At that February 2018 sale, the work fetched £49.8 million (approximately $68.7 million); the winning bidder was Harry Smith, the London-based chairman of the art advisory firm Gurr Johns, who purchased it along with three other Picassos from the sale. It had changed hands only once before that auction: After Picasso’s death, his estate sold it to an unknown private collector.

Picasso’s Femme nue couchée depicts his muse Marie-Thérèse Walter reclining in a state of sensual abandon. The fluid brushwork, vivid contrasts of color, and radically distorted biomorphic forms lend the female body an almost sculptural presence. The Château de Boisgeloup in Normandy, where the painting was created, provided a studio for Picasso’s experiments with form and three-dimensional work.

The painting remained in Picasso’s collection until his death, then with his heirs until 2008, when it entered a private collection. Offered publicly for the first time, it headlined Sotheby’s Modern Evening Auction in New York on May 17, 2022. With an estimate reported at approximately $60 million, it achieved $67.5 million including fees; the hammer price was $58.5 million. The result made it the evening’s top lot.

Hidden from the public for almost 40 years, Dora Maar au chat portrays Picasso’s muse seated in a chair with a black cat on her shoulder. The painting was first acquired by Paris dealer Pierre Colle in 1946 and was later owned by Chicago collectors Leigh and Mary Block.

In 2006, Chicago’s Gidwitz family decided to auction the painting at Sotheby’s New York, where it sold for $95.2 million, almost twice the $50 million low estimate. Sotheby’s granted the family a $53 million guarantee in order to secure the painting, a rarity at the time.

At the evening sale, five bidders competed for the work. Reportedly among them were casino magnate Steve Wynn, Ohio retailer Leslie Wexner, and Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen. But the portrait of Maar went instead to an eager bidder in the room wielding a paddle with the number 1340, in an unusually visible move for a transaction of that level at a marquee auction.

The sale drew speculation as to the identity of the winning bidder, with many suspecting that he was an ultrawealthy collector from Russia. Ultimately, it was revealed that the anonymous floor bidder bought the work for the Georgian mining tycoon Bidzina Ivanishvili. New to the art world at the time, Ivanisvhili, who would go on to serve as Georgia’s prime minister, has a modern and contemporary art collection worth $1 billion, most of which he keeps in storage in London, with replicas of his masterpieces adorning his Tbilisi residence.

Leading Christie’s 20th-century art evening sale in New York in May 2020, Picasso’s Femme assise près d’une fenêtre (Marie-Thérèse) from 1932 sold for $103.4 million, almost double the $55 million pre-sale estimate. After a 19-minute long spar between six bidders, the painting finally sold to a bidder on the phone with Vanessa Fusco, Christie’s co-head of the 20th-century art evening sale, in a moment that proved the art market had returned in full force after a period of economic lag caused by the coronavirus pandemic.

Before its sale at Christie’s, it was last exhibited at Paris’s Picasso Museum showcase “Picasso 1932, année érotique” in 2017, alongside mega-collector Steven Cohen’s 1932 Picasso portrait Le Rêve, which he purchased for $155 million in 2013. The following year, Femme assis went to the Tate Modern in London for an exhibition titled “The EY Exhibition: Picasso 1932, Love Fame Tragedy.”

The work is notable both for its large size, and in its unusual depiction of Picasso’s muse, Marie-Thérèse Walter, who is often portrayed as sleeping or dreaming. Here, she is sitting upright in a chair, as if enthroned with her gaze directed at the viewer. The most striking aspect of the piece, Fusco told ARTnews ahead of the sale, is “the incredible presence of this woman and the agency which he’s given her, which you don’t always see in his depictions of her.”

Picasso’s painting of a seated Parisian teenager smoking a pipe and wearing a crown of roses is a signature work from the artist’s Rose Period and it is one of the works from this era that remains in private hands.

In May 2004, the work was offered at an evening sale in New York by Sotheby’s, alongside 33 other pieces from its owners Mr. and Mrs. John Hay Whitney to raise funds for the Greentree Foundation, the family’s charitable organization. The anonymous bidder, who purchased it for $104.1 million (well above the $70 million pre-sale estimate), beat out six others who were vying for it that evening.

The Whitneys had purchased it from a Zurich-based dealer for around $30,000 in 1950. The buyer is believed to have been Guido Barilla, the billionaire heir and chairman of the Barilla pasta company. When it sold in 2004, Garçon à la pipe became the most expensive ever sold at auction, beating out Van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890), which had sold for $82.5 million in 1990. Garçon à la pipe held that record until May 2010.

In May 2010, the star lot of an evening sale of Impressionist and modern art at Christie’s New York was Picasso’s Nude, Green Leaves and Bust, from his 1932 series of paintings of Marie-Thérèse Walter. During the sale, eight bidders competed for the work, driving the hammer well past the $70 million expectation. It ultimately sold for $106.5 million to a phone bidder.

Held in private hands for 60 years, the painting was sold by Los Angeles philanthropist Frances Lasker Brody, who had purchased it with her husband, Sidney F. Brody, from New York dealer Paul Rosenberg in January 1951 for $17,000.

The sale of Peggy and David Rockefeller’s art collection at Christie’s New York, which included top lots by Paul Gauguin, Edouard Manet, Henri Matisse, and Claude Monet, set a historic high for a single-owner sale in 2018. The piece that fetched the highest price was Picasso’s portrait Fillette a la corbeille fleurie, made during the artist’s Rose Period.

The work’s first owners were Leo and Gertrude Stein, the American siblings and early patrons of modern art, who bought it from a Paris dealer the year it was completed. After Gertrude Stein’s death, the painting was passed to her companion, Alice B. Toklas, whose estate sold it in 1968 to a syndicate of collectors associated with the Museum of Modern Art in New York. David Rockefeller then purchased it for himself.

When the painting sold for a staggering $115 million during the blockbuster Rockefeller auction in 2018, its price wasn’t the only reason the piece attracted attention. Featuring a nude prepubescent girl, wearing only a necklace and holding a basket of red flowers, the work generated controversy over Picasso’s sexualized image of a child, known among historians to be an underage flower seller and sex worker named Linda.

The work has long been considered a masterpiece, though. “She represents the themes that Picasso would wrestle with for his life—love, sex, beauty, tenderness, violence,” said Marc Porter, chairman of Christie’s Americas. Since the record sale of the work, criticism among scholars surrounding Picasso’s treatment of women has persisted. In 2021, protesters staged a demonstration outside Barcelona’s Picasso Museum in an attempt to bring attention to the issue.

In La Femme à la montre, Marie-Thérèse Walter appears elegantly dressed, wearing a wristwatch and sitting in an armchair against a blue background. The painting features bright colors, geometric shapes, and a harmonious composition. Her affair with Picasso remained secret for years because the artist was married to Olga Khokhlova. The wristwatch may symbolize the passage of time and the complexity of their romance.

In 1966, collector Ernst Beyeler purchased the painting directly from Picasso’s studio in Mougins, France. Two years later, Emily Fisher Landau acquired it. It remained a centerpiece of her collection for nearly 50 years, displayed above the fireplace in her Manhattan residence until her death in 2023. On November 8 of that year, Sotheby’s auctioned the painting in New York for $139.4 million, making it Picasso’s second-most expensive artwork sold at auction, after Les Femmes d’Alger (Version “O”).

In 1956, the legendary Picasso collector Victor Ganz put in an offer to buy all 15 pieces in Picasso’s Delacroix-inspired “Les Femmes d’Alger” series (1954–55) from Paris dealer Henry Kahnweiler for $212,500. In years to follow, Ganz kept just five from the group after selling the rest of them to recoup his purchase price; Version “O” was among the few he held on to.

Decades later, in 1997, Christie’s staged the blockbuster sale of Ganz’s prized Picasso collection in New York, where the piece went for $31.9 million to London dealer Libby Howie, who is said to have purchased it on behalf of a buyer in Europe. Nearly two decades later, at Christie’s New York in May 2015, Version “O” resurfaced on the market and set a record price of $179.4 million, making it the most expensive work to sell at auction at the time. Reported to have been purchased by the Qatari royal Al Thani family, that painting remains the most expensive Picasso ever to be auctioned.

KIFF's redesigned logo feels fresh and alive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Film festivals don't have a direct impact on most people's lives. Few of us actually get around to attending one, and the films they feature rarely reach our nearest arts cinema, let alone the local multiplex. Yet, whether we ever buy a ticket to one, film festivals really do matter.

This is where new talent, both in front of and behind the camera, gets to show people what they're made of; where fresh and off-the-wall ideas get their first airing in public. A typical festival is a bubbling cauldron of visual styles, storytelling techniques and new voices, which will then gradually filter into mainstream cinema, advertising, music videos and more.

Occasionally too, a festival hit will break out in its own right. Reservoir Dogs started its journey at Sundance; Parasite at Cannes. Even if you've seen neither film, you'll have felt their ripple effects on culture in general.

Wth all that heated experimentation and ambition, you'd think a film festival logo would be another canvas for creativity. But too often, these events seem to just throw together a bunch of elements (a camera, a film reel, a clapperboard) without much thought. So it was a pleasant surprise to see the logo for the Kolkata International Film Festival (KIFF) does something very different.

Kolkata, formerly known as Calcutta, is the capital of West Bengal in India. This year the 32nd edition of its annual film festival runs from 16 to 23 December. Recently, its organisers revealed this new logo (shown above), which is the work of Sandip Ray.

Sandip is not only a filmmaker himself, he's also the son of the legendary Satyajit Ray: a director who was also a designer working on book covers, film posters and typefaces. And in this logo, Sandip has done his father proud.

Where the typical film festival logo juggles several references, this one commits to a single idea, and is all the better for it. Heavy black letters are cut into by burnt-orange triangles, each edged with sprocket holes like a strip of film.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

If someone had described that to me before I'd seen it, I'd probably have thought "That sounds awful". Film strips are the clip art of cinema: as big a cliché as a popcorn box, and increasingly anachronistic to boot.

But here, the execution is everything. Crucially, Sandip hasn't used the film strips as decoration of the logo, but as its foundation. They're not just a way of adding interest to the logo design; they are the logo design. It's the difference between committing to an idea and not actually having one in the first place.

To my mind, the triangles could be seen as doubling up as play and rewind buttons… although admittedly this might just be me.

Overall, the important thing about this logo is that it doesn’t look like anything else. I've spent so many years looking at perfectly formed sans serifs that it's made me weary. And the idea that more and more people are going to use AI tools that serve up an average of this style depresses me even more.

KIFF’s logo, in contrast, is chunky, angular and a bit odd. Some people might dislike it for that very reason. But I love the fact that two colours and one bold idea are all it needs to be instantly recognisable, and that’s got to be an inspiration for logo designers everywhere.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9143. London’s Photographers’ Gallery to launch exhibition programme for emerging voices

The Photographers’ Gallery has become increasingly reliant on ticket sales as a source of income, its director says

© Dennis Gilbert. Courtesy of the Photographers’ Gallery

The Photographers’ Gallery in London is launching a 10-year programme to platform emerging talent through a series of biennial exhibitions. The initiative has been made possible by what the not-for-profit gallery describes as “a very generous grant” from the UK-based John Kobal Foundation.

Shoair Mavlian, the director of the Photographers’ Gallery, declined to specify how much the grant is worth, but she tells The Art Newspaper that it will cover all the costs of staging the shows in its second-floor space, newly named the John Kobal Foundation Gallery.

The initiative will see one artist selected every two years for an exhibition. The first solo exhibition will be announce later this year and will run from 23 June to 26 September 2027.

“The whole idea of the programme is based around giving an opportunity to someone who hasn’t had an institutional solo show before,” she says. “The Photographers’ Gallery is in a similar situation to all other museums in the UK in that we are pressured into having to always do blockbuster shows [to generate revenue]. And what this programme allows us to do is to take risks.”

The gallery received a renewed three-year grant from Arts Council England in 2023, as one of the funding body’s national portfolio organisations (NPO). This grant represents around 20% of the gallery’s revenue, says Mavlian, however, it has remained the same throughout years of rising operational costs and high inflation, and so like other UK arts organisations, the gallery has become more reliant on other sources of income. Its accounts for the year ending 31 March 2025 report £620,573 in admissions income, which is more than two thirds the value of its NPO grant within a single year.

“We are under this constant pressure to sell tickets and bring people through the door—which, of course, is important. But what that means is we then don’t always see the full breadth of photography that is being made today. We are often looking at things that are historic rather than looking at the contemporary.”

The John Kobal Foundation was established in 1990 a year before the death of the eponymous film historian and photography collector “to advance the public appreciation and awareness of photography”.

“We are delighted to support this important new initiative," says Michael Mack, the co-chair of the John Kobal Foundation, “which honours John’s vision of nurturing creativity and innovation in photography.”

#9142. Contemporary Stained-Glass Windows Installed in Notre-Dame, Spanish Man Awarded $1.12 M. for Renaissance Door Discovery, and More: Morning Links for November 10, 2026

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

WINDOW OF OPPORTUNITY. New stained-glass windows by French artist Claire Tabouret have been quietly installed in the Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral and will be unveiled to the public on December 7, reports Le Figaro. The project, backed by French President Emmanuel Macron, has faced controversy, but has moved forward against all odds, overcoming one legal challenge while still facing another. The six new windows feature a color-rich, figurative telling of the story of the Pentecost and have been placed along the nave’s southern aisle. The windows were made with the Simon-Marq workshop in Reims and for now, they are reportedly hidden behind red curtains. Meanwhile, heritage groups have opposed the project because it requires the removal of existing 19th-century stained-glass windows designed by Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc, who intended them as part of a cohesive homage to Gothic architecture. Related Articles Chicago Crowds Try and Fail to Move Anish Kapoor's Bean, Art Lawyer Michael Ward Stout Has Died, Louvre President Says Mona Lisa's Move Will Be Sad, and More Lucien Smith Cause of Death Announced, French Authorities Investigate Unauthorized Reproductions of Picasso Silver Plates and Gold Medallions, and More: Morning Links for November 6, 2026

BRINGING HOME THE CANADIAN BACON. Things are looking up for Canadian artists who are still grappling with US tariffs. The country has just proposed a federal budget that exempts artists from paying taxes on C$45,000 ($38,000) of their earnings, reports The Art Newspaper. “In Budget 2026, we’re backing the Canadian artists who tell our stories,” wrote Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in a November 5 social media post. “That means if you’re a Canadian artist, you won’t pay tax on up to C$45,000 of income derived from your creative work,” he added. And that’s not all; the proposed budget also pledges C$783.1 million ($554 million) over five years to the National Arts Centre, Library and Archives Canada, the National Battlefields Commission and national museums. Visitors under 25 will also get free entry to national museums, thanks to C$46.3 million ($32.8 million) in subsidies for the same five years, followed by C$11.5 million ($8.1 million) per year. Not to be forgotten, the Canada Council for the Arts will get C$20 million ($14.1 million) over three years. However, some tell TAN the funding is still short of what is needed. “As a sector, we still have a lot of questions, while many artists need relief now,” said Jenna Faye Powell, interim national executive director of Carfac (Canadian Artists’ Representation/Le Front des Artistes Canadiens).

The 4 a.m., August 28, 1963, handwritten final draft of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr’s historic “I Have a Dream” speech is being offered for sale at Christie’s New York to benefit charity on January 22, 2027. [ArtDependence]

In an open letter appealing to the Nuremberg City Council, a contemporary arts association has warned of the possible closure of the 1967-founded Kunsthalle Nürnberg amid a strained public budget. [Monopol Magazine]

Artist Olafur Eliasson is partnering with ARoS Aarhus Art Museum in Denmark to create a publicly accessible study space and library containing research materials about Eliasson’s practice, opening alongside a major solo exhibition dedicated to him, plus newly installed artwork and more. [Ocula]

Artist Ryan Gander dishes on the YBA’s “egocentric, attention-seeking, shallow kind of art.” Plus, the act of drawing and painting being “futile and dumb,” despite including several of his own new paintings in his latest show, “Maybe: Ryan Gander” at Towner gallery in Eastbourne. [The Guardian]

WHEN ONE DOOR CLOSES … A decade after, Juan Francisco León Catena, a resident of Úbeda in southern Spain, chanced upon a magnificent Renaissance doorway hidden behind the walls of his property under renovation—he will be awarded a €1 million prize ($1.12 million) for his trouble, reports El País. Following a long legal battle, León Catena is poised to receive the award, granted by the Spanish Historical Heritage Law for chance, significant artistic finds. In this case, that find is a 15th-century portal from a former hospital church designed by Spanish Renaissance architect Andrés de Vandelvira. Discovered in excellent condition, experts deemed it of “great aesthetic value” and a unique Renaissance artwork. However, the local Andalusian Regional Government initially refused to pay up in a case that made its way to the High Court of Justice of Andalusia, which ultimately rejected their arguments. Now, León Catena is in talks with the city of Úbeda on how to best promote the heritage site, and there is the additional question of surrounding, city-owned buildings that also house the relic but are in dire need of restoration and risk collapse.

What did those poor kids do to offend HBO's graphic designers?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In case you hadn't heard, there's a new Harry Potter series on the horizon. This December we're all hopping back on board the Hogwarts Express, only this time it's on TV, with HBO planning to serialise the entire book series over the next few years. The trailers so far have drawn sharp scrutiny – which you might expect, given the popularity of the films. And now, a new series of character posters is raising eyebrows.

What did those poor kids do to upset the editor of these posters? The designs each feature one of the principal cast members' faces in close-up, with their wand held aloft in front of it. Their faces are effectively cut in half by the wand, and some feel they look bizarrely stretched. Poor Ron seems to have been particularly afflicted. Not only that, but each half of the faces appears to be lit by a different light source, making the whole thing look weirdly spliced together. Suffice to say, these aren't among the best print ads we've seen.

New posters for HBO’s ‘HARRY POTTER’ series. Premieres December 25 on HBO. https://t.co/T8xqd9MCNDNovember 9, 2026

"Unfortunately, this is the first major mistake since the beginning of the marketing campaign. It’s already receiving a lot of negative reviews on the official pages. I’m shocked they released it like this, especially after how flawless the attention to detail has been from the very beginning," one Redditor comments. Another adds, "Each poster looks like they took one half of their face from two different photos and combined them along their wands. Absolute terrible editing work, imo."

And to add insult to injury, fans have quickly knocked together an improved take on the design, focussing on just one half of each characters' face. These are arguably more striking and dramatic, and, more importantly, the faces don't look distractingly wide.

Time will tell whether the series lives up to the books, or the original film series. But one thing's for sure: these aren't among the best posters of the year, let alone all time.

#9140. Julia Stoschek Collection to Celebrate 20 Years with ‘Selfish in Bed’ Exhibition and Düsseldorf Reopening

Sarah Lucas doesn’t appear particularly apologetic in her 2000 self-portrait Selfish in Bed II. Standing with her hands on her hips, the British artist wears a black T-shirt with the words “SELFISH IN BED” printed across the front. Next April, that cheeky photograph will set the tone for a major group exhibition celebrating the 20th anniversary of the Julia Stoschek Collection in Düsseldorf, Germany.

Aptly titled Selfish in Bed, the exhibition opens on April 10, 2027, and will bring together 52 works by 43 artists, including Tracey Emin, Bill Viola, Wolfgang Tillmans, and Bruce Nauman. Selfish in Bed marks the inaugural exhibition of the reopened Julia Stoschek Foundation’s Düsseldorf headquarters, which closed for renovations in April 2025. Related Articles This LA Exhibition of Julia Stoschek's Video Art Collection Is the City's Hottest Ticket  Sarah Lucas Wins New Museum's $400,000 Sculpture Prize

Curated by Krist Gruijthuijsen, the director of Finland’s EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art and former director of Berlin’s KW Institute for Contemporary Art, the show looks at how we construct our identities, express our sexuality, and present ourselves to the world.

The exhibition takes the bed as its starting point. It’s a place increasingly of contradictions: It’s private and vulnerable, yet inter-connected, where we spend hours scrolling through the images and opinions that shape how we see ourselves. The show explores that tension through works spanning the late 1960s to the present, including several that the foundation has never exhibited before.

There are more than a few highlights. Emin’s Why I Never Became a Dancer (1995), Simon Fujiwara‘s Joanne (2016/2018), and Hannah Wilke’s Through the Large Glass (1976), all explore women’s relationships with their bodies, sexuality, and public image. Meanwhile Monica Bonvicini‘s Destroy She Said (1998) challenges traditional domestic roles, and Ed Atkins’s Us Dead Talk Love (2012) examines questions of identity and authenticity in the digital age.

The exhibition is set to span two floors, and include video projections, mirrored surfaces, glass walls, and television monitors creating an immersive environment. Works by Viola, Tillmans, and Rosemarie Trockel will be presented together in a grouping that explores the human experience from birth onward.

For Stoschek, whose collection now includes more than 1,000 works by over 300 artists, the anniversary is also an opportunity to reflect on two decades of collecting.

“I am a very emotional collector,” Stoschek said in a statement. “An artwork has to get under my skin. I need images that stay with me.”

The Düsseldorf headquarters, housed in a converted industrial building dating to 1907, has undergone an extensive renovation by Berlin architecture firm Kuehn Malvezzi, which originally adapted the space for exhibitions in 2007. In Berlin, the foundation closed its exhibition space at the end of October after a decade of programming, shifting its attention toward Düsseldorf and international projects.

A publication marking the collection’s 20th anniversary will accompany the exhibition, with contributions from writers and critics including Rachel Cusk, Chris Kraus, Dean Kissick, and McKenzie Wark.

Selfish in Bed will run from April 10 through December 19, 2027, with an opening reception on April 9.
