#9104. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9103. Ontario house by Brian O'Brian takes cues from farm buildings

Canadian architect Brian O’Brian has completed a rural weekend house in Ontario that features a slanted, corrugated-metal facade and an angled roof covered with greenery.

The Hemlock House sits on a 72-acre (29-hectare) property in the southern town of Markdale.

The project grew in scope over time. Originally, the plan was to renovate an old farmhouse, but the client ultimately decided to create an entirely new house.

“What started as a modest renovation evolved into a full replacement of the small, 1930s farmhouse,” said Brian O’Brian, a Toronto-based architect.

The commission came about after the client saw another project by O’Brian in the area – a 19th-century schoolhouse with stone walls that had been converted into a cottage.

For the Hemlock House, O’Brian took cues from the region’s agrarian buildings to conceive the design.

Set on a flat site surrounded by woods and farmland, the house is composed of a long bar and adjoining box, and totals 3,250 square feet (302 square metres).

A long entry driveway “traces the lineage of the site”, passing by an old farmhouse and century-old barn.

The new house draws upon these earlier buildings and “extends the language of agricultural buildings into a contemporary domestic form”, the architect said.

The home’s bar-shaped volume is topped with a sloped, metal-clad roof, while the attached box has an angular green roof.

The north side of the house is lined with a slanted wall made of corrugated metal.

Cut into the wall are three windows, which can be covered by external, perforated steel panels that slide up and down. This elevation also features a boxy protrusion with wood cladding.

“This is meant to feel like an agrarian building at first view, but one that begins softening and opening on approach,” said the architect.

The southern elevation – which overlooks patios and a swimming pool – features hemlock siding and ample glazing. Various roof overhangs help shield the building from sun and snow.

The house also has a carport, which is sheltered by a canopy made of wood and metal.

Within the home, there is a division between public and private spaces.

The linear volume, which spans two levels, contains a principal suite, a secondary suite, and two bedrooms with a shared bathroom. The adjoining box holds a kitchen, dining area and living room.

Rooms feature neutral colours and a mix of earthy and industrial materials.

“Concrete and hemlock define every surface, carrying a steady material logic through the house,” the architect said.

Other projects in Ontario include a 1970s chalet that was renovated and expanded by UUfie to conform to its steep site, and a black cabin by Barbora Vokac Taylor that includes wedge-shaped clerestory windows.

#9101. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

the built99 guide documents, celebrates, and preserves architectural intelligence from india, revealing how these practices -- and architects -- are progressing the future of our built environment.

What if the architecture in India could lead the world in sustainable, deeply human design? A comprehensive new book highlights this possibility. The inaugural Built99 guide and its companion digital directly, below, explores the future of the built environment by documenting 99 carefully selected Indian architecture and design practices. Rather than simply cataloging past achievements, this expansive volume experiments with an ongoing global dialogue, translating decades of regional research, material ethics, and civic impact into a permanent print edition. The guide examines the foundational, forward-thinking ideas driving each studio’s portfolio.

By elevating these 99 practices onto an international stage on both designboom and ArchDaily, the Built99 guide documents, celebrates, and preserves architectural intelligence from India and the Global South. #9099. Concept car that transforms from SUV to pickup is "a symbol of freedom" says Fiat CEO

Fiat’s new Multiplay concept car can transform from an SUV into a pickup, with movable seats and a flexible interior designed to accommodate different uses, explains the brand’s CEO Arnaud Belloni in this exclusive video interview produced by Dezeen.

“We are reinventing here the concept of family car,” said Belloni, describing the vehicle, which was unveiled at the 2026 Paris Motor Show.

Measuring 4.45 metres long, Multiplay combines the passenger space of a multi-purpose vehicle (MPV) with the raised stance of an SUV and the open cargo area of a pickup.

A sliding rear section allows the vehicle to switch between configurations, changing its enclosed passenger compartment into an open load bed.

The concept takes inspiration from the original Fiat 600 Multipla, launched in 1956, which accommodated six people within a body measuring just 3.5 metres long.

“Basically, that car invented the concept of multipurpose vehicle – the MPV,” said Belloni, referring to the original model.

The new Multiplay revisits this approach through a series of movable components. Its seats can be repositioned to accommodate different passenger and cargo arrangements, while the rear spoiler rotates to become an integrated bicycle rack capable of carrying two bikes.

“Multiplay can slide from an MPV to an SUV to a pickup,” said Belloni. “That, I would say, is a symbol of freedom.”

In its family configuration, the car accommodates six passengers alongside an additional modular seat.

The pickup configuration provides an open load bed for carrying bicycles, sports equipment and other bulky items.

Inside, a multifunctional unit called the Petsenger seat can be used to accommodate a pet, mount a child car seat or serve as a small table.

The front passenger seat can also turn towards the rear to create a reclining Sunseat, which uses the dashboard as a backrest and sits beneath a panoramic roof.

The interior uses a contrasting palette of red and pink, set against bright green exterior bodywork inspired by the colours of a watermelon.

Its textiles were made using a stitch-free, three-dimensional knitting process, while a digital display integrated into the dashboard disappears when the vehicle is switched off.

Multiplay was presented alongside Multiplina, a separate three-metre-long electric concept with four seats and two doors, as part of Fiat‘s wider exploration of urban and family transportation at the car show.

The company describes Multiplay as a testing ground for future design solutions rather than a preview of a specific production model.

“Fiat is obsessed with all types of mobility on each size of car. So whatever the size, we are able to invent new categories of vehicles,” said Belloni.

Founded in Turin in 1899, Fiat is an Italian automotive manufacturer producing passenger cars and commercial vehicles, from compact city cars to larger family vehicles.

This video was produced for Stellantis as part of a partnership. Find out more about our partnership content here.

#9098. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#9097. Design Doha Biennial 2026 set to explore how traditional crafts can shape the future of design

Design Doha Biennial 2026 opens in Doha, Qatar, today, bringing together more than 19 exhibitions, five installations and over 80 designers, featuring projects that use traditional water systems and building techniques to tackle urban heat.

Following a postponement earlier this year due to war in the Gulf, the event will now run from today until 31 January 2027, with its opening programme taking place from 5 to 7 November.

For the event Doha‘s historic neighbourhood of Fereej Al Asmakh has been transformed into an exhibition venue to showcase contemporary architecture and design from across the Middle East, north Africa and south Asia.

The biennial features more than 19 exhibitions across over 20 countries, alongside five permanent public design commissions, talks and awards. Many of the exhibitions occupy restored courtyard houses in Fereej Al Asmakh, where installations sit within the neighbourhood’s existing buildings and outdoor spaces.

At the centre of the biennial is Arab Design Now 2026, a group exhibition curated by Palestinian architect Noura Al Sayeh that brings together 81 designers, artisans and makers.

The exhibition includes 78 new commissions and 17 films, presenting finished objects alongside the people, materials and processes involved in making them.

“The second edition of Arab Design Now, the headline exhibition of the Design Doha Biennial, puts context in the foreground,” said Al Sayeh.

“It showcases design alongside the designers themselves, as well as the related environments, processes, artisans, craftsmen and makers.”

Other highlights include The Sower, an exhibition by Mexican designer Fernando Laposse featuring a living seed bank developed in Qatar.

Another exhibition called Post-Oil 2026 examines how industrial materials such as concrete, glass, steel and aluminium have shaped the built environment of the Gulf.

Five public design commissions will also be installed in Fereej Al Asmakh, reinterpreting traditional construction methods and environmental techniques for contemporary urban settings.

These include Salsabil, a cooling structure by French architecture studio New South that uses ceramic spheres and fine mist to create cooler areas in public spaces, as well as Palm Construct, a shaded pavilion by Emirati architect Abdalla Almulla that combines palm wood with traditional weaving techniques.

Dezeen will be reporting from Doha throughout the opening, visiting the exhibitions and public installations to bring readers the highlights of this year’s programme.

The team will also be speaking to Design Doha director Fahad Al Obaidly and Arab Design Now curator Noura Al Sayeh, alongside participating architects and designers, to explore the ideas and processes behind the exhibitions.

Design Doha was established in 2024 by Qatar Museums under the leadership of its chairperson, Sheikha Al Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani.

The inaugural edition featured more than 300 designers and studios across 24 exhibitions and attracted more than 118,000 visitors, establishing the biennial as a platform for contemporary design from the region.

Design Doha 2026 takes place from 5 November until 31 December in Doha, Qatar. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

#9095. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#9094. "Commitment of the design community remains strong" say Ukrainian design week founders

Photography courtesy of Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week

This year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week went ahead despite Russian strikes affecting the local design community. The event’s founders share their top picks of exhibited brands that have continued production amid the war.

“The reality of operating in Ukraine remains extremely challenging,” Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week founders Anatolii and Kateryna Roskovshenko told Dezeen.

Ukraine has endured the constant threat of Russian bombardment for over four years, and recent months have been increasingly deadly for civilians, according to Human rights group Amnesty International.

Daily life for Ukrainians continues to be upended. Designers and manufacturers are navigating keeping operations running as Russian strikes damage their warehouses.

“Air raid alerts, power outages, disrupted logistics, rising costs, and damage to production facilities directly affect everyday operations,” said the husband-and-wife duo. “Several major Ukrainian furniture manufacturers have had their production facilities and warehouses hit by Russian strikes, causing significant damage and disrupting their work.”

“Businesses often have to adjust their schedules at short notice, reconsider investments, and find alternative ways to maintain production. Some have been forced to scale back operations or temporarily suspend projects,” they continued.

In the face of this, the design community came together for this year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, which took place in Kyiv from 5 to 11 October.

The flagship Design Hall exhibition gathered two hundred Ukrainian brands across interiors, furniture, decor, lighting and product design, showcasing their work to thousands of visitors.

Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, which joined the international community of World Design Weeks in 2023, made changes to its planned programme to keep attendees safe. During the event, Kyiv experienced attacks that interrupted electricity and water supplies.

“Several planned events had to be cancelled for security reasons, while some furniture brands were unable to participate following earlier attacks on their facilities,” said the Roskovshenkos.

“We adapted Design Hall to take place entirely indoors, with changes to the original programme.”

“Yet the commitment of the design community remains strong,” they continued. “Thousands of people attended Design Hall, and hundreds of designers, manufacturers, and creative professionals came together to exchange ideas, establish new connections, and support each other’s work.”

Design brands in Ukraine are exploring new ways of developing products, testing materials and reaching customers, according to the Roskovshenkos.

“Despite the challenges of working during the war, Ukraine’s design industry continues to evolve,” they said. “Collaboration has become an essential part of how the industry operates, helping businesses share knowledge, find new opportunities, and adapt to uncertainty.”

“Particularly encouraging is the fact that new Ukrainian design brands continue to launch, even as existing businesses navigate difficult circumstances.”

“Over seven seasons of Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week, we have witnessed this evolution firsthand,” the pair continued. “Brands are becoming more confident in their identity, finding new niches, rethinking their production processes, and developing products that reflect their own creative vision.”

Read on for Anatolii and Kateryna Roskovshenko’s highlights from this year’s Ukrainian Design and Innovation Week:

“Juniper is a Ukrainian brand that combines traditional Carpathian craftsmanship with contemporary design, working with natural materials such as sheep’s wool and wood.

“In collaboration with KredoBank, the brand has created a collection of four wall panels inspired by Ukraine’s distinctive landscapes.

“Through natural textures and handcrafted techniques, each piece captures the character and atmosphere of these places, bringing elements of Ukraine’s cultural and natural heritage into contemporary interiors.”

“Gushka is a Ukrainian wool textile manufacturer [that] preserves traditional craftsmanship, creating its products on historic weaving looms using age-old techniques and natural wool from sheep that graze freely on the Carpathian slopes.

“Kint is a Kyiv-based furniture and object design brand [that] specialises in creating original furniture, decor, and accessories for residential and commercial spaces.

“The first collaboration between Kint x Gushka, initiated in 2024, brings together contemporary furniture design and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship. The result is a limited-edition series of armchairs, reimagining kint’s signature design through natural Carpathian wool and Gushka’s traditional textile techniques.

“The two versions feature different handcrafted finishes – Stranded uses hand-applied wool strands layered over a smooth base to create a distinctive textured surface, and Brushed is made by hand-combing wool using a traditional smooth-weaving technique, resulting in a softer texture.”

“KosKa is a Ukrainian brand working with recycled paper-based biomass, combining traditional handcrafting techniques, material experimentation, and contemporary artistic expression.

“Founder Kateryna Kostevych creates each object by hand, exploring the possibilities of sustainable materials and bringing together natural textures, tactile qualities, contemporary forms, and functionality.

“The featured objects include Trypillian Bull, an original interpretation of ancient Trypillian ceramic figurines, and two lamps named Hat and Bright Eye.”

“Tiini is a Ukrainian brand that creates lighting, furniture, and accessories, born at the intersection of tradition and modernity.

“The brand breathes new life into authentic crafts, harnessing the richness of materials and their interaction with light to create unique pieces for the home.”

“Venko is a Ukrainian design and production workshop founded in 2014 in Radyvyliv.

“The brand specialises in creating three-dimensional wooden wall panels and decorative pieces, with a particular focus on textures and the expressive qualities of natural materials.”

“Yalanzhi Objects is a Ukrainian brand of lighting and decorative objects founded in 2019 by Yuliia and Yevhen Melnychenko. The brand approaches light as an artistic medium, not merely a functional element, but a way to shape spaces, establish rhythm, and create an emotional focal point within an interior.

“Many of its pieces are crafted from Zemletsvit, the brand’s signature biocomposite – a natural material characterised by tactile surfaces, earthy tones, and a distinct handmade quality.

“Yalanzhi Objects combines contemporary design language, sculptural forms, and a thoughtful connection to Ukrainian culture.”

#9093. GTA VI takes over miami with six real-life cars built by west coast customs

from a pink-and-purple sports coupe to a police-liveried supercar, the fully drivable lineup turns fictional automotive excess into something with actual horsepower.

Rockstar Games has brought six vehicles from Grand Theft Auto VI out of the screen and onto the streets of Miami, enlisting Los Angeles-based West Coast Customs to transform fictional designs into fully drivable machines. The project arrives ahead of the game’s November 19 release, translating some of its most recognizable automotive creations into physical vehicles. From classic American lowriders to contemporary supercars, the collection recreates the exaggerated personalities that have long defined the franchise’s approach to car culture.

The six vehicles retain their fictional brand names, distinctive silhouettes and elaborate finishes, with modifications extending well beyond their exterior appearance. Each has been presented alongside its digital counterpart, revealing how closely the real builds follow their virtual references. Photographs also place the collection at recognizable Miami landmarks, including Herzog & de Meuron’s 1111 Lincoln Road parking structure and the Miami Marine Stadium. The locations connect the actual city with Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional interpretation of Florida’s coastal metropolis.

Among the six creations developed by Rockstar Games in collaboration with West Coast Customs, the Grotti Cheetah draws on the proportions of classic Italian supercars, with a low-slung body, sculpted side intakes and a naturally aspirated 4.9-liter V8 engine. The customization workshop finishes the vehicle with a gradient paint treatment, lowered suspension and custom leather upholstery. The Invetero Coquette takes a more contemporary direction, pairing a 6.2-liter V8 with a striking pink-and-purple camouflage exterior. Meanwhile, the Progen Emerus embraces track-inspired engineering, combining a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 with aerodynamic bodywork, an oversized rear wing and a bright orange interior.

American automotive culture provides the references for the Albany Buccaneer and Albany Manana. The former reinterprets a 1960s lowrider with candy-green metallic paint, gold wheels, air suspension and zebra-patterned interior details. The Manana follows a different tradition, adopting the dramatically elevated stance of a donk-style custom car, complete with oversized wheels, blue bodywork and gold accents. Completing the lineup is the Pegassi Tempesta, a V10-powered supercar dressed in the fictional Vice Beach Police Department’s black-and-white livery. Apparently, even law enforcement gets a supercar in Leonida.

The project reflects the close relationship between Grand Theft Auto’s visual identity and real-world automotive customization. Throughout the series, Rockstar Games has developed fictional manufacturers and vehicles that borrow recognizable proportions and styling cues from established brands while exaggerating their defining characteristics. Translating these designs into functional machines requires more than reproducing their shapes. Paint finishes, wheel proportions, suspension setups and interior materials become essential to preserving the identity of each vehicle beyond the screen.

The resulting collection also highlights the influence of Miami’s automotive culture on the fictional world of Vice City, from extravagant lowriders to brightly colored performance cars. By placing the vehicles in the same urban environment that inspires the game, Rockstar Games brings its digital references back to their physical origins. With Grand Theft Auto VI scheduled to launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19, the six builds offer an unusually tangible preview of its universe, where even the most improbable designs appear perfectly at home on the road.

#9092. Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

Joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

“No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

For much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

You can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of users on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift shows up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

But perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

As Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Plan B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

“I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”

The practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo says. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

Of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

“Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”

In 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a new career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

“I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

Rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

Recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

But that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

#9091. Six standout projects unveiled at Designart Tokyo 2026

As the 10th anniversary edition of Designart Tokyo gets underway, Jane Englefield reports on six highlights from the citywide festival of Japanese creativity.

Designart Tokyo opened on 30 October and will remain open across Tokyo until 8 November.

Around 150 projects by exhibitors from 13 countries are on display at various galleries and other pop-up locations throughout the city.

This year’s main exhibition venue is the former site of the Tokyo Expressway, also known as the KK Line, a portion of which is now an elevated park in the heart of Ginza.

Designart Tokyo’s first dedicated design store is also located on site, selling works from brands including Nendo and Alessi, as well as designers Ronan Bouroullec and Kwangho Lee.

Read on for six of our highlights from the event:

Pulling Apart is a novel adhesive on display as part of the Daikanyama exhibition Separation: Designed to Come Apart, which includes various products created to allow for fluid disassembly and recycling.

Tokyo studio Nomura created the project with the knowledge that, when glue-based adhesives are applied to timber or metal, they are often difficult or impossible to remove. This can mean that materials suffer indelible marks or cannot be recycled at the end of their life.

Nomura’s adhesive is a strong but flexible tape, which firmly holds heavy materials in place. But once the tape is tugged, it stretches and comes away easily.

“Leave one end within reach behind the plinth or under the tabletop, and when the time comes, a single pull undoes the whole thing,” said Nomura.

The tape was developed with easy-disassembly bonding technology developed by Aica Kogyo Company and is still in the prototype phase.

“Peco poco” is a common Japanese onomatopoeia describing a growling stomach.

Experimental design studio Howdunit used the phrase as its starting point for this table lamp, which can be manually unfolded like an accordion thanks to a small hook built into the top of the shade.

Made from delicate layers of gauzy textile, the light opens with a “rhythmic ‘peco poco’ motion” and can be set at various heights.

“By continually asking how things are made, we aim to discover new possibilities in design,” said Howdunit founders Haruto Kamijo and Sho Tasaki.

Forest: Perspectives by Oji Holdings and We+

Tokyo paper manufacturer Oji Holdings is presenting an exhibition in Ginza that meditates on our perspectives on forests.

The manufacturer asked nine professionals, from designers and wood specialists to a writer and a chef, to visit the network of forests it manages and share their individual responses to the landscape.

Among them are delicately whittled spoons made from fallen branches and wood sheets crafted out of bark using a process similar to making washi paper.

The exhibition was laid out in an encyclopedic display designed by local studio We+, founded by Toshiya Hayashi and Hokuto Ando.

Founded in 2021, Tokyo-based 21B Studio is presenting an exhibition at Shibuya’s brutalist-style Tiers Gallery.

Box is the first solo show by the young studio, conceived to demonstrate the myriad ways we can create the humble paper box through various folds and incisions.

The studio is giving out an intricately designed flatpack poster advertising the exhibition, which, once assembled, resembles the geometric architecture of Tiers Gallery itself.

Over in Tokyo Midtown, design master’s student Cecil Nabenashi is presenting a playful exhibition of vases and bowls made of deep-fried paper and fibres.

Nabenashi looked to tempura, Japanese food that is coated in batter and deep-fried in oil, when creating the project.

His goal was to experiment with his “tempura” technique to see if it could provide a long-lasting finish for design objects, using a “batter” he developed from a specially developed blend of non-edible ingredients.

The designer told Dezeen that he plans for his next challenge to be a deep-fried garment.

Industrial Romanticism is an exhibition on display at Minato’s Axis Gallery, Japan’s first dedicated design gallery founded in 1981.

The show is a group exhibition held by designers Yoshiki Matsuyama and Ryota Yokozeki, who asked eight leading Japanese companies to take part.

In-house designers at each of the companies, including bathroom brand Toto and camera maker Fujifilm, created prototypes of recognisable products with an imaginative twist.

Among the designs is a piano made by Ryusuke Baba of musical instrument maker Yamaha. Baba created the piano from pieces of timber that would normally be rejected for an instrument, creating a keyboard with an offbeat sound.

Designart Tokyo 2026 takes place from 30 October to 8 November 2026 at various locations across Tokyo, Japan. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9090. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#9089. Lagoons will weave through new Egyptian city masterplanned by SOM

International architecture studio SOM has unveiled plans for a new city in Egypt named Alam Al Roum, which will stretch 7.2 kilometres along the Mediterranean coastline.

Set to be built near Marsa Matrouh, the 20.6-square-kilometre masterplan features swimmable lagoons alongside 22 kilometres of seawater-connected lagoons, which will weave through the built environment to support stormwater management.

“The Mediterranean is home to some of the world’s great cities, shaped over centuries by climate, culture and economic forces,” said SOM principal Thomas Hussey.

“Alam Al Roum presents a rare opportunity to imagine a new city from the ground up, one that responds to the realities of climate change while offering an exceptional quality of life.”

SOM designed the masterplan around Egypt’s north coast landscape and climate, orienting buildings and public spaces to take advantage of coastal breezes and sunlight.

The development will be elevated to accommodate changing coastal conditions, while waterfront areas will be protected with natural interventions such as riparian buffers, stormwater wetlands, stabilised dunes and living shorelines.

Designed for developer Qatari Diar, Alam Al Roum will comprise beachfront and lagoon-side neighbourhoods, town centres, areas for hospitality and resorts, golfing facilities, an education district and a business hub.

A grand boulevard will form an urban spine connecting an international marina on the Mediterranean Sea with a mobility hub further inland.

Aiming to establish the city as a year-round cultural destination, Alam Al Roum’s waterfront downtown will contain a cultural pier, lighthouse, amphitheatre, yacht club, mosque, and markets.

The first phase of the city development is expected to commence in 2030, comprising a four-square-kilometre area with a beachfront stretch, open-sea-connected lagoons and a town-centre marina.

“Alam Al Roum represents our vision for a new generation of Mediterranean destinations – one that goes beyond the traditional seasonal resort to create a vibrant, year-round coastal city,” said Qatari Diar CEO Hamad bin Talal Al-Thani.

“We are bringing together nature, the sea, hospitality and everyday life within a carefully planned environment that reflects the unique character of Egypt’s north coast,” he continued.

“Through our partnership with SOM and our global network of experts, we are creating a destination that is rooted in its landscape and climate, while setting a new benchmark for integrated coastal development in the Mediterranean.”

In recent years, Egypt established a new capital city east of Cairo. The initial design concept for the city was designed by SOM and further developed by the international building consultancy Dar al-Handasah Shair & Partners.

#9088. 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That said, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

“In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your big day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely shows empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”

#9087. designboom listens: objects of common interest embraces the beauty of unexpected contrasts

from new order and talking heads to aphex twin and david bowie, the athens- and new york-based design studio shares the songs that shape its creative mood, evoke memories, and offer unexpected parallels with the way it approaches design.

For Objects of Common Interest, design and music share an interest in bringing different elements together to create something unexpected. The Athens- and New York-based studio, founded by Eleni Petaloti and Leonidas Trampoukis, works across objects, interiors, and spatial installations, exploring how form, color, material, and perception can shape the way we experience our surroundings. Their playlist moves between emotional melodies, hypnotic repetition, and experimental sounds, echoing the different qualities they explore through design.

This relationship also comes through in the latest public installation by the studio, titled Out of This World – A Field of Conditions, presented in the Miami Design District. Bringing together six different conditions that alter how people perceive and experience their surroundings, the series of interactive sculptures explores the possibility of seeing familiar environments in new ways. Music offers a similar point of departure in the duo’s playlist, which moves between New Order, Talking Heads, Chet Baker, Gorillaz, Aphex Twin, and David Bowie. Some selections bring back particular atmospheres or memories, while others help shift perspective, break creative blocks, or focus attention on the smallest details. Read on for the duo’s answers and discover the tracks that accompany their practice.

What song best captures your creative practice? Objects of Common Interest (OoCI): Bizarre Love Triangle – New Order. We like the coexistence of emotion, structure, repetition, and unexpected energy. Different elements come together in a way that feels both precise and unpredictable. There is something about that tension that relates to how we approach design.

What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project? OoCI: This Must Be the Place – Talking Heads. It has an effortless optimism that we love. It’s familiar but somehow always feels fresh. A good reminder that inspiration doesn’t necessarily come from looking for something extraordinary, but from seeing ordinary things differently.

Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past? OoCI: Let’s Get Lost – Chet Baker. There’s something incredibly nostalgic about Chet Baker’s voice. It takes us back to a certain atmosphere rather than a specific moment, a feeling of being somewhere between the past and the present.

What song is stuck in your head right now? OoCI: Coming Up Roses – Harry Styles. Sometimes a song just stays with you, without needing a particular reason.

What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track, the one you secretly know every word to? OoCI: On Melancholy Hill – Gorillaz. It has this beautiful balance of melancholy and optimism. Dreamy, slightly strange, and incredibly addictive. Perfect for those late hours when you’re tired but don’t really want to stop working.

What song do you put on when you are stuck and need a breakthrough? OoCI: Love to Angie – Red Astaire. Sometimes the best way to move forward is to stop overthinking. Music can shift your energy completely, and suddenly things start making sense again.

What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you are making right now? OoCI: What Else Is There? – Röyksopp. We love its slightly mysterious atmosphere and the way it builds tension. We wouldn’t say music directly influences the forms we create, but it definitely influences the mood and energy around the process.

What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details? OoCI: Avril 14th – Aphex Twin. It’s incredibly simple and delicate. Every note feels intentional, and the space between the notes is just as important. It reminds us how much can happen through very little.

If people would wear headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing? OoCI: Tainted Love – Soft Cell. There’s something wonderfully theatrical and slightly eccentric about it. It has a strong personality, a certain strangeness, and an irresistible rhythm. We like the idea of experiencing our work with that kind of unexpected soundtrack.

What is your favorite album cover art? OoCI: Power, Corruption & Lies – New Order. We love the unexpected relationship between a classical painting of flowers and a coded graphic system. It brings together something deeply romantic and something almost scientific. Two seemingly unrelated languages coexist and create an entirely new identity.

What is a track that best describes your favorite project you have worked on so far? OoCI: Sound and Vision – David Bowie. For Out of This World – A Field of Conditions, our latest public installation in the Miami Design District. The project brings together six different conditions that alter how we perceive and experience our surroundings. We like how the song suggests a world where sound, color, and imagination coexist. It captures that sense of curiosity and the possibility of experiencing something familiar in an entirely unexpected way.
